docs.title: VIRA Documentation
docs.text: VIRA is a self-hosted, local-first context and tool server for AI agents. It gives agents private access to your devices, memory, data and MCP tools, with permissions and an audit trail in your hands. It also ships a control center, chat workspace, memory, durable workflows and specialist agents.

docs.title: Two pieces
docs.text:
Piece What it is Where it runs VIRA Server API, dashboard, chat, agents, tools, memory, database, scheduler, admin Docker container (Linux, macOS, Windows) VIRA Link Device companion: collectors, offline ledgers, sync, command polling Android, iOS (unsigned), web/PWA, Linux, Windows and macOS (Apple Silicon). Intel Macs use the web/PWA build.

The browser dashboard and chat are served by VIRA Server and need no separate install. VIRA Link is only needed on devices whose signals you want to collect.

docs.title: How these docs are built
docs.text:
The documentation is Docs-as-Code: every page is Markdown in this repository, reviewed in the same pull request as the code it describes. CI builds the HTML site you are reading and generates the PDF manuals from the exact same sources — there is no separately maintained copy.

  • HTML — rebuilt on every push to main
  • PDF — VIRA User Manual and VIRA Developer Manual, rebuilt on every release and attached to GitHub Releases
  • API reference — generated from the FastAPI OpenAPI schema, so it cannot drift from the code

See Contributing for how to add or change a page.

docs.title: Current priority: Phase 1 — Positioning and proof
docs.text:
The immediate goal is a clear public story and a reproducible five-minute demo:

  1. Say what VIRA is today, who it is for, and what is not built yet.
  2. Prove the working path with a real Chatbot + tool + read-only database demo.
  3. Publish the security and privacy evidence.
  4. Keep the roadmap and repository metadata in sync.

See Five-minute proof and Security overview.

docs.title: Local development loop
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python run.py

The server starts on http://localhost:8000. API docs are available live at /docs and /redoc.

To preview this documentation site locally:

./scripts/docs.sh serve

The script creates a project-local .venv with the docs toolchain, so it does not depend on a system-wide mkdocs. Open http://127.0.0.1:8001. Use ./scripts/docs.sh build for a strict build and ./scripts/docs.sh pdf for both PDF manuals.

docs.title: Agent and tool platform
docs.text:
Phase 5 makes the agent platform measurable and reviewable. This page is the developer reference for generated artifacts, budgets, memory ranking, run recovery, cost budgets and observability.

Research basis and evaluation design: evaluation research basis. Current results: agent platform evaluation.

docs.title: Generated tools and agents
docs.text:
Generated artifacts always follow:

draft → approved → enabled
        ↘ rejected
enabled → disabled → enabled

A draft never executes. Both the tool runtime and the agent runner re-check the stored status and approved_at on every invocation, so disabling or rejecting an artifact takes effect immediately even if a registry still holds an old tool object.

docs.title: Create a draft
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/generated \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "kind": "tool",
    "name": "weather_lookup",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "description": "Look up a city forecast",
    "spec": {
      "type": "http",
      "method": "GET",
      "url": "https://api.example.com/weather",
      "allowed_hosts": ["api.example.com"],
      "parameters": {"city": {"type": "string", "required": true}},
      "query": {"city": "{city}"},
      "response_format": "json"
    }
  }'

Generated tools are intentionally narrow:

  • one HTTPS GET;
  • no custom headers, tokens or request bodies;
  • an explicit host allow-list;
  • public-address SSRF checks;
  • JSON output validation when response_format is json;
  • bounded response size.

docs.title: Create a draft agent
docs.text:
{
  "kind": "agent",
  "name": "brief_writer",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Writes a short evidence-based brief",
  "spec": {
    "system_prompt": "You are a careful briefing agent. Use the allowed tools and never invent facts.",
    "tools": ["rag_search", "web_search"],
    "max_steps": 4,
    "temperature": 0.2
  }
}

An enabled agent runs through POST /api/v1/generated/{id}/run with a bounded AgentLoop, the allow-listed tools and the configured step budget.

docs.title: Review and enable (administrator)
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/generated/{id}/approve
POST /api/v1/generated/{id}/enable
POST /api/v1/generated/{id}/disable
POST /api/v1/generated/{id}/reject   {"reason": "..."}
GET  /api/v1/generated

Every transition is audited. The dashboard Agents → Generated tools and agents view exposes the same actions.

docs.title: Tool budgets and safety
docs.text:
Control Where Default Max tool steps agents[].config.max_steps 6 Per-tool timeout tool_timeout 90 s Whole-run observation budget max_total_tool_chars 30,000 chars Wall-clock budget max_seconds 240 s Per-run tool-call budget max_steps + loop repeat guard — Destructive approval security.approvals enabled Output clipping loop + generated JSON validation —

When a budget is exhausted the loop stops calling tools and writes the best answer from the observations it has. It never silently continues forever.

docs.title: Memory ranking and user controls
docs.text:
Memory retrieval uses a transparent score:

0.55 * relevance
+ 0.20 * importance
+ 0.15 * recency (30-day half-life)
+ 0.10 * agreement
+ feedback bonus (useful +0.15, not_useful -0.35)

Muted memories are excluded from both lexical and vector retrieval. Retrieval marks last_used_at and increments use_count.

User controls:

POST /api/v1/memories/{id}/feedback   {"useful": true, "note": "current"}
POST /api/v1/memories/{id}/feedback   {"useful": false}
POST /api/v1/memories/{id}/feedback   {"muted": true}
DELETE /api/v1/memories/{id}

The evaluation suite covers single-session recall, multi-session recall, knowledge updates, recency, abstention and feedback.

docs.title: Run recovery and observability
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/runs?status=failed lists a user's runs. A failed or interrupted run can be resumed without duplicating the original user message:

POST /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/resume

At API startup, queued/running runs are marked failed with interrupted by server restart, so they become visible and resumable instead of looking active forever. The dashboard Agents → Recent agent runs view shows status, failure reason, a redacted trace and a Resume action.

GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/timeline returns:

  • run status and failure reason;
  • thinking/tool/check events;
  • tool inputs and results with secret-looking values redacted;
  • bounded previews.

Chat already streams the same events live and stores the trace with the answer.

docs.title: Cost and token budgets
docs.text:
Quota scopes are user, agent, org and global, with day or month periods. Agent quotas let you cap a specific agent independently of the user.

PUT /api/v1/admin/quotas
{
  "scope": "agent",
  "subject_id": "chat",
  "period": "month",
  "token_limit": 500000,
  "cost_limit_usd": 5
}

The usage dashboard shows token/cost totals, per-model and per-agent breakdowns, quota consumption and the quota form (including agent scope).

docs.title: Agent templates
docs.text:
Built-in specialist definitions now include:

  • incident_triage — evidence-based server/device triage;
  • research_brief — local RAG + public web evidence with citations;
  • data_steward — read-only inventory and data-quality answers;
  • plus the existing researcher, critic, insight_coach, study_coach and device_doctor.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
python3 scripts/evaluate.py --write
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_phase5 -v

The report includes tool-selection top-1/top-3, task completion, memory abilities, failure recovery, destructive-action guards and run recovery. It is deterministic, runs twice for repeat stability, and records the git revision so releases can be compared.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are open and welcome. VIRA is modular: you can work on one sensor, agent, tool, API route or documentation page without understanding the whole codebase.

Canonical guide

The full contributor guide lives at CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository root. This page adds the documentation-specific rules and the local preview workflow.

docs.title: Get running locally
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA.git
cd VIRA
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# optional: local model
ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

python run.py

The dashboard is at http://localhost:8000. On first run, admin credentials are printed to the terminal.

docs.title: Documentation rules
docs.text: Documentation is Docs-as-Code. Every page lives in docs/ as Markdown and is reviewed in the same pull request as the code it describes.

docs.title: Where does a page go?
docs.text:
The site follows Diátaxis. Pick exactly one purpose:

Kind Audience Location Tutorial / how-to End users docs/user/ Explanation / architecture Developers docs/dev/ Reference Both docs/reference/ Design document Developers docs/dev/designs/ Roadmap Developers docs/dev/roadmap/

Do not add loose Markdown to the repository root. If a page does not fit, open an issue before writing it.

docs.title: Write and preview
docs.text:
./scripts/docs.sh serve      # http://127.0.0.1:8001
./scripts/docs.sh build      # strict build, same as CI

The script creates a project-local .venv with the docs toolchain. Do not run the system mkdocs binary directly: it may not have Material installed and will fail with No module named 'material'.

The build is strict in CI, so broken internal links or missing nav entries fail the pull request.

docs.title: Front matter
docs.text: Every page starts with a single H1. The title is taken from it; no front matter is required. Use sentence case for headings.

docs.title: Images and diagrams
docs.text:
• Put images in docs/assets/ and reference them relatively (assets/foo.svg).
  • Prefer SVG for architecture diagrams.
  • Prefer Mermaid fenced blocks for new diagrams so they render in both HTML and PDF:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Sensor --> EventBus --> Agent --> Tool
```

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
• Link other pages with relative .md paths: [Plugin SDK](../dev/plugin-sdk.md).
  • Link source files with full GitHub URLs, not relative paths.
  • Do not link to a heading that does not exist; the build fails.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
A pull request that changes public behaviour, configuration or an extension point is not done until:

  • [ ] the matching page under docs/ is updated, and
  • [ ] mkdocs build --strict passes locally, and
  • [ ] new pages are added to nav in mkdocs.yml.

The docs workflow builds the site and both PDFs on every push and pull request. On main it deploys a versioned site with mike; on a v* tag it publishes that version and attaches both PDFs to the GitHub release.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text:
A lightweight architecture decision record (ADR) log. Each entry records the context, the decision, alternatives and consequences. Propose a new entry with the Decision proposal issue template.

Status values: Proposed, Accepted, Superseded, Rejected.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Live stream plus relay for agent notifications
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Proactive agents need to reach users outside the API. VIRA is self-hosted, so requiring a cloud push provider for every install would break the local-first story. At the same time, an app-closed mobile device cannot keep a long-lived stream.

Decision: Use a two-path delivery model. VIRA Link keeps an authenticated NDJSON notification stream open while it is connected and shows native OS notifications from it. For app-closed or multi-process delivery, schedules can use the push channel; device tokens are forwarded to a configurable relay that can speak FCM/APNs or another gateway. Webhook and push channels share retries, dedupe and audit.

Consequences: the default install works without cloud credentials and still has native alerts while the client runs. Remote delivery is explicit configuration. Multi-replica API deployments must use the relay rather than the per-process stream.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Proactive schedules run inside the agent orchestrator
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: The five daily-use agents need recurring triggers, delivery and safety. A separate cron-style worker would duplicate the agent runtime, lose tool/permission parity and create a second place to load agents.

Decision: Add a ProactiveScheduler owned by AgentOrchestratorModule. It claims due rows from agent_schedules atomically, resolves agents from the existing AgentRegistry, and executes a typed TaskRequest through RuntimeScheduler.run_task(). Every run records a durable timeline and an agent_schedule_runs row. Notifications go through the existing notification queue; in-app is immediate and external delivery uses a webhook provider in the worker.

Consequences: scheduled runs share chat's identity, tools, approvals, quotas and audit. Multi-process deployments need the database claim/lock to remain atomic (SQLite transaction or Postgres row locking). Delivery providers beyond webhook (FCM/APNs) can be added behind the same notification contract without changing schedules or agents.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Paper-aligned agent architectures, single-agent default
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (Kim et al., 2025) evaluated five coordination topologies (single, independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid) across 180 matched configurations. Multi-agent systems were not uniformly better: results ranged from +81% to −70% versus a single agent, sequential tasks degraded under every MAS variant, and independent agents amplified errors 17.2× versus 4.4× for centralized coordination.

Decision: Add reusable architecture bases in vira/agent/architectures.py and export them from vira.agent. Keep SingleAgent as the default. Encode the paper's selection rules in recommend_architecture(): sequential/non-decomposable and high-baseline tasks stay single-agent; tool-heavy and dynamic tasks may use decentralized coordination; decomposable analysis uses centralized coordination with a validation pass; hybrid is reserved for tasks that need both hierarchy and peer review. Worker counts, debate rounds and LLM calls are bounded, and every run records an architecture/coordination block.

Consequences: developers can choose a topology by subclassing a base class or let AdaptiveAgentSystem select one from a task profile. Multi-agent coordination is opt-in, observable and budgeted. Local models keep the single-agent default unless a caller supplies evidence that coordination helps.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — One BaseAgent, with an LLMAgent layer
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: VIRA had two BaseAgent implementations and ChatAgent reimplemented tool discovery, permissions, prompting, the tool loop, delegation and history. Read-only tools were rejected because the executor always checked the execute action, MCP tools were only half-wired, and per-conversation history lived in a class-level dict shared by every instance.

Decision: Make vira/agent/base.py the only BaseAgent (lifecycle, task contract, per-task identity, helpers, tool policy) and add vira/agent/llm_agent.py for LLM/tool agents. ChatAgent becomes a thin subclass handling only chat events, history and responses. Tool permission actions are resolved from each tool's declared permissions. Any permitted tool, including qualified MCP tools, may be called by name even when it was not in the prompt's selected subset.

Consequences: one lifecycle and one authoring model; new agents are a class with an execute method plus a tool policy. BaseAgent.initialize rejects classes without execute. The legacy think/plan/act/reflect pipeline and the example/sensor agents were removed; ChatAgent is the only shipped agent.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — One scoped knowledge store, not RAG per agent
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Agents need to persist what they learn so it can later feed a single dynamic AGI knowledge base. Per-user or per-agent vector stores would multiply indexes, break deduplication and conflict resolution, and tie knowledge to ephemeral runtime identifiers (BaseAgent.agent_id is a random UUID).

Decision: Keep one knowledge store keyed by rows tagged with scope ∈ {conversation, personal, agent, org, global} plus scope_id. Retrieval takes the set of scopes a caller may read and merges results with uploaded documents and episodic memory. Agent scope uses a stable role name, not the runtime agent id. Corrections append revisions; only the promotion pipeline creates global knowledge.

Consequences: shared learning, one embedding pipeline and one place to enforce isolation. Isolation depends on correct scope filtering, so read paths must be scope-aware and tested. Physical partitioning by scope remains a later scale optimisation, not a design primitive.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — SQL as the knowledge record, NoSQL as derived indexes
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: The knowledge base needs multi-row transactions (dedupe, supersession, events) and scope/ACL filtering. Retrieval also needs vector, lexical and possibly graph indexes, which may be better served by NoSQL systems. Choosing one database for both concerns would limit the framework either way.

Decision: Separate the authoritative record from derived stores. Items, revisions, provenance and scope live behind the KnowledgeRepository port (SQLite now, PostgreSQL at scale). Embeddings live behind VectorIndex; caches behind KnowledgeCache. Both are rebuildable and never authoritative. The factory selects adapters from config.yaml, and every adapter must pass the same conformance suite.

Consequences: a future Qdrant, OpenSearch, Redis or graph backend is an adapter plus a config change, not a rewrite. Writes must keep the record and derived indexes consistent (outbox or synchronous update). The team must resist reading derived stores as if they were authoritative, and must keep SQL confined to adapters.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Local-first, single-process by default
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: VIRA targets a self-hosted machine or NAS. Users want private data and a short install path, not a hosted service.

Decision: SQLite and an in-process event bus are the default. PostgreSQL, external brokers and a separate worker are optional scale-out paths. The API, worker, scheduler and dashboard remain deployable on one host.

Consequences: simple installs and easy backups; horizontal scale requires PostgreSQL/Redis and the worker. Hosted SaaS is an explicit non-goal for now.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Python core, not a Rust rewrite
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: The roadmap defers a Rust rewrite until profiling proves Python is the bottleneck and extension APIs are stable.

Decision: Keep the Python core. Optimise with bounded work, workers and durable queues before considering a rewrite.

Consequences: faster iteration and a large contributor pool; no low-level performance win.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Approval gates for destructive actions
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Prompt injection and model mistakes make unrestricted shell, filesystem and sandbox calls unsafe for a first-run product.

Decision: Destructive calls create a single-use, expiring approval request. Execution requires an explicit user/admin decision. Approval state is re-checked at execution time.

Consequences: safer defaults and an audit trail; some agent flows need a human step. Approval is not a sandbox or a formal policy engine.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Generated artifacts are declarative and approval-gated
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Generated tools/agents are a Phase 5 research-adjacent capability. Unreviewed generated code is unacceptable.

Decision: Generated tools support one declarative HTTPS GET with a host allow-list; generated agents use an allow-listed tool set and a step budget. Artifacts move through draft → approved → enabled, and drafts never execute.

Consequences: safer and testable generated capabilities; richer generated code and formal verification remain future research.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Native macOS target, web/PWA for Intel
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: The client matrix lacked macOS while the server already ran there through Docker.

Decision: Add a native Flutter macOS target and publish an unsigned Apple Silicon artifact. Intel Macs use the documented web/PWA client. Signing and notarization are owner/deployment work.

Consequences: native macOS support for Apple Silicon; Intel support has an explicit alternative rather than a separate artifact.

docs.title: 2026-11-21 — Monthly release cadence with deterministic evaluation
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Releases and quality claims need to be predictable and comparable.

Decision: Target a monthly release, keep a Keep-a-Changelog file, validate tags against the changelog, and record deterministic evaluation results with each release.

Consequences: repeatable release notes and measurable regressions; live model quality still needs the separate benchmark.

docs.title: How to claim one
docs.text:
1. Open the matching issue and comment that you are taking it.
  2. Read CONTRIBUTING.md and the linked code.
  3. Make the smallest change that satisfies the acceptance check.
  4. Open a PR with the test output and any docs updates.

Maintainers aim to give an initial response within three business days. If an issue is stale or no longer accurate, say so in the issue rather than working around it.

docs.title: VIRA Plugin SDK
docs.text: VIRA plugins are normal Python packages that declare a manifest. A plugin can add tools, HTTP routes, sensors, agents, prompt-defined specialists, event handlers, scheduled jobs and namespaced state without importing kernel internals.

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
my-plugin/
├── vira-plugin.json
└── plugin.py

{
  "id": "acme.weather",
  "name": "Weather Tools",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "api_version": "1",
  "description": "Weather lookup and forecasts.",
  "author": "Acme",
  "license": "MIT",
  "homepage": "https://example.com/weather",
  "entrypoint": "plugin.py:WeatherPlugin",
  "permissions": ["tools.register", "http.routes", "storage"],
  "categories": ["weather", "productivity"],
  "requires": {"vira": ">=0.2.0"},
  "config": {"units": "metric"}
}

vira-plugin.toml and plugin.json are also accepted. The entrypoint can be plugin.py:Class or module:Class for a pip-installed package.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
from vira.plugins.api import Plugin

class WeatherPlugin(Plugin):
    async def setup(self, ctx):
        # register everything here
        ...

    async def start(self):
        ...

    async def stop(self):
        ...
  • setup(ctx) runs once before start.
  • start() starts background work.
  • stop() releases resources. Scheduled tasks and event subscriptions are also cancelled by the manager.
  • A failed plugin is isolated: it is marked error, other plugins still load.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The manifest must declare every capability used. The server allow-list can deny a permission, in which case the plugin is not loaded.

Permission Allows tools.register read-only tool registration tools.register.write tools with write/execute/admin actions sensors.register collector/sensor registration agents.register runtime agent and prompt-definition registration events.read subscribe to kernel events events.publish publish kernel events http.routes mount an API router storage namespaced key/value state and data directory jobs.schedule periodic async jobs config.read read manifest config

Server policy lives in plugins.allowed_permissions, plugins.denied_permissions and plugins.allow_write_tools in config.yaml.

docs.title: Registering a tool
docs.text:
from vira.tools.base import BaseTool, ToolPermission, text_result

class ForecastTool(BaseTool):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(
            name="acme_forecast",
            description="Get a weather forecast for a city.",
            permissions=ToolPermission(actions=["read"]),
            input_schema={
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                "required": ["city"],
            },
        )

    async def execute(self, city: str = "", **kwargs):
        return text_result(f"Sunny in {city}")

ctx.register_tool(ForecastTool()) makes the tool available immediately. It appears in the tool catalog, in tool_search, and in agent prompts on the next request. Use qualified_name= to namespace it.

docs.title: HTTP routes
docs.text:
from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter()

@router.get("/status")
async def status():
    return {"ok": True}

ctx.register_router(router)

Every plugin router is mounted at:

/api/v1/ext/<plugin-id>/...

Authentication is the plugin's responsibility. Use the shared dependencies if you need a user; document the routes and validate input carefully.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
def factory(sensor_config, event_bus, dispatcher, metrics):
    return MySensor(...)

ctx.register_sensor("my_sensor", factory, {"interval": 30})

Plugin sensor events use the same validated ingestion path as built-in sensors. The server-local device identity is applied automatically.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Runtime agents must subclass vira.agent.base.BaseAgent:

agent_id = await ctx.register_agent(MyAgent(ctx.runtime))

Prompt-defined specialists are simpler and safer:

from vira.agent.definitions import AgentDefinition

ctx.register_agent_definition(AgentDefinition(
    name="weather_brief",
    description="Use for weather briefings.",
    prompt="You are a concise weather briefer. Use the forecast tool.",
    tools=["acme_forecast"],
    max_steps=3,
))

They are removed automatically when the plugin is disabled or unloaded.

docs.title: Events and jobs
docs.text:
async def on_event(event):
    ...

ctx.on_event("device.battery.state", on_event)

async def sweep():
    ...

ctx.schedule(sweep, interval_seconds=300, run_immediately=True)
await ctx.emit("acme.weather.updated", {"city": "Pune"})

docs.title: State and data
docs.text:
ctx.set_state("last_city", "Pune")
city = ctx.get_state("last_city", "London")

path = ctx.data_dir / "cache.json"   # ./data/plugins/<plugin-id>/

State is SQLite/PostgreSQL-backed and namespaced per plugin.

docs.title: UI contributions
docs.text:
A manifest can advertise a small front-end contribution without shipping code into the core admin bundle:

"ui": {
  "slots": ["settings", "dashboard"],
  "entry": "/ui/panel.js",
  "style": "/ui/panel.css",
  "label": "Weather"
}

GET /api/v1/plugins/ui returns active contributions with the plugin's mount prefix (/api/v1/ext/<plugin-id>), so an admin shell can load the script or open the route. Mount scripts only from trusted plugins and keep them free of secrets.

docs.title: Managing plugins
docs.text:
Administrator API:

GET    /api/v1/plugins                 list discovered/loaded plugins
POST   /api/v1/plugins/discover        rescan configured directories
GET    /api/v1/plugins/sdk             SDK/API metadata
GET    /api/v1/plugins/{id}
POST   /api/v1/plugins/{id}/enable
POST   /api/v1/plugins/{id}/disable
POST   /api/v1/plugins/{id}/reload
DELETE /api/v1/plugins/{id}            forget record (files are kept)

Enabling, disabling and reloading take effect without restarting the server for tools, agents, event handlers and jobs. New HTTP routers are mounted at startup; restart to add or remove route modules.

Configuration:

plugins:
  directories:
    - ./examples/plugins
  allow_write_tools: true
  denied_permissions: []
  data_dir: ./data/plugins

VIRA_PLUGIN_PATH adds colon-separated directories. Packages can also expose a vira.plugins entry point.

docs.title: Reference plugins and MCP example
docs.text:
The repository maintains three complete plugin examples and one MCP server example, all covered by vira/tests/test_examples.py:

Example Demonstrates examples/plugins/hello_world read-only tool, HTTP route, persisted state examples/plugins/reading_list read/write tools, route, state, prompt specialist examples/plugins/focus_budget event subscription, scheduled job, tool, route examples/mcp/notes_server.py real MCP stdio server with tools and a resource

Run them with:

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_examples -v

docs.title: Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
• api_version is the SDK contract. This server supports "1".
  • Bump a plugin's version for every release.
  • requires supports a small semver subset: >=, >, <=, <, ==, ^, ~, comma-separated ranges and *.
  • Declare {"vira": ">=0.2.0"} when a plugin needs newer core APIs.
  • Plugin dependencies are loaded first and cycles are refused.

docs.title: Security guidance
docs.text:
• Request the smallest permission set.
  • Never load remote code at runtime.
  • Do not log secrets or raw device events.
  • Return errors as data; do not crash the host process.
  • Treat plugin code as trusted local code: plugins run in-process.

docs.title: Release process and cadence
docs.text: VIRA targets a monthly release on the first Tuesday, with patch releases as needed for security or broken installs. The cadence is a target, not a promise that every month needs a feature release.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
  • Server tags: vX.Y.Z (for example v0.5.0).
  • Server prereleases: vX.Y.Z-rc.N (for example v0.5.0-rc.1).
  • Client tags: vira-link-vX.Y.Z (for example vira-link-v1.2.0).
  • Do not put build numbers in public tags. Rebuilds use a new patch version.
  • vira.__version__ is the server source of truth.
  • client/pubspec.yaml is the client source of truth.
  • Breaking API/config changes require a minor or major bump and a migration note.

The release workflows use different tag prefixes so a client release cannot trigger the server workflow.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md follows Keep a Changelog:

  • keep an ## [Unreleased] section at the top;
  • add user-visible changes under Added / Changed / Fixed / Security;
  • move entries into ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD when tagging;
  • never rewrite a released section except to correct a factual error.

docs.title: Release assets
docs.text:
Server releases:

vira-X.Y.Z-source.tar.gz
vira-X.Y.Z-checksums.txt
vira-X.Y.Z-release-manifest.json

Client releases:

vira-link-X.Y.Z-android.apk
vira-link-X.Y.Z-ios-unsigned.zip
vira-link-X.Y.Z-web.zip
vira-link-X.Y.Z-linux-x86_64.AppImage
vira-link-X.Y.Z-windows-x64.zip
vira-link-X.Y.Z-macos-arm64.zip
vira-link-X.Y.Z-checksums.txt

Asset names are lowercase, versioned and stable. The release workflow verifies that every expected artifact exists before publishing.

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text:
1. Confirm the roadmap phase and evaluation results are current.
  2. Regenerate the deterministic evaluation:
python3 scripts/evaluate.py --write
  1. Run the full backend suite:
python3 -m unittest discover -s vira/tests -q
  1. Run python3 -m vira doctor against a clean install.
  2. Update CHANGELOG.md, vira.__version__, docs and the security page.
  3. Validate the release locally:
python3 scripts/release_tools.py check vX.Y.Z
python3 scripts/release_tools.py notes vX.Y.Z
  1. Commit, tag and push:
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "VIRA X.Y.Z"
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The Release workflow validates the tag/version/changelog, runs the full suite, builds the source archive and checksums, generates release notes from the standard template and publishes the GitHub release.

  1. For VIRA Link, run Build VIRA Link with the client version, verify every platform artifact and checksums, then enable create_release.
  2. Announce the release with the demo link, evaluation result and any migration steps.

docs.title: Release tool commands
docs.text:
# Validate a server or client tag
python3 scripts/release_tools.py check vX.Y.Z
python3 scripts/release_tools.py check vira-link-vX.Y.Z --product client

# Preview the standard release body
python3 scripts/release_tools.py notes vX.Y.Z
python3 scripts/release_tools.py notes vira-link-vX.Y.Z --product client --dist dist

# Verify assets and write the checksum file
python3 scripts/release_tools.py assets vX.Y.Z --dist dist --write-checksums

# Machine-readable release manifest
python3 scripts/release_tools.py manifest vX.Y.Z --dist dist

docs.title: Hotfixes
docs.text:
For a security or install-blocking bug:

  1. branch from the released tag;
  2. bump PATCH and add a ### Security or ### Fixed entry;
  3. run the same checklist;
  4. tag and publish;
  5. backport to main if main has moved on.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text: Architecture and product decisions are recorded in the decision log. A release should link any decision that changed public behaviour.

docs.title: Response targets
docs.text:
• Security reports: private triage within 2 business days.
  • Bugs and install failures: initial response within 3 business days.
  • Good first issues and feature proposals: initial response within 5 business days.
  • Releases: monthly target, with a written note when a month is skipped.

These are targets, not contractual SLAs.

docs.title: Agent architectures
docs.text:
VIRA ships the five coordination topologies evaluated in Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (Kim et al., 2025). The point of the paper is not "add more agents". It is that architecture must match the task: performance ranged from +81% to −70% relative to a single agent across the same models and tools.

The base classes live in vira/agent/architectures.py and are exported from vira.agent.

docs.title: What the paper found
docs.text:
Effect Result What VIRA does about it Tool-coordination trade-off Tool-heavy tasks pay a large coordination tax (β ≈ −0.33); more agents can be worse. recommend_architecture() never defaults to multi-agent for tool-heavy or sequential tasks. Capability ceiling Above ~45% single-agent accuracy, extra agents usually lose (β ≈ −0.41). Profiles with a baseline ≥ 0.45 select SingleAgent. Error amplification Independent agents amplified errors 17.2×; centralized coordination contained them to 4.4×. CentralizedAgentSystem runs a validation pass before synthesis; IndependentAgentSystem is documented as high-risk. Task contingency Centralized gained +80.9% on parallel analysis; decentralized gained +9.2% on dynamic navigation; all variants lost 39–70% on sequential planning. The selector is rule-based and conservative, falling back to a single agent.

Measured coordination costs used by the profiles:

Architecture Topology Overhead vs single Error amplification SingleAgent one reasoning locus 0% 1.0× IndependentAgentSystem parallel workers, synthesis only 58% 17.2× CentralizedAgentSystem orchestrator + isolated workers 285% 4.4× DecentralizedAgentSystem peer-to-peer debate 263% 7.8× HybridAgentSystem orchestrator + peer review 515% 5.1×

docs.title: Base classes
docs.text:
from vira.agent import (
    SingleAgent,
    IndependentAgentSystem,
    CentralizedAgentSystem,
    DecentralizedAgentSystem,
    HybridAgentSystem,
    AdaptiveAgentSystem,
)

Every class extends LLMAgent, so it keeps prompts, tool policy, memory, knowledge, progress events and response handling. Only the coordination loop differs.

docs.title: SingleAgent — the default
docs.text:
One reasoning locus and one tool loop. Use it for sequential tasks, tool-heavy work, high-baseline tasks, and anything without clear evidence for coordination.

class SupportAgent(SingleAgent):
    name = "support"
    system_prompt = "Answer support questions from the local knowledge base."
    tools = {"allow": ["knowledge_search", "rag_search"]}

docs.title: IndependentAgentSystem — parallel ensemble
docs.text:
Runs worker_count workers with no inter-worker communication, then synthesizes. Cheapest multi-agent option, but the paper measured the highest error amplification. Use it for diverse first drafts, not for correctness-critical work.

class Brainstorm(IndependentAgentSystem):
    name = "brainstorm"
    system_prompt = "Generate distinct, well-reasoned options."
    worker_count = 3          # clamped to 1..8

docs.title: CentralizedAgentSystem — orchestrator + validation
docs.text:
The orchestrator decomposes the task, workers run independently, the orchestrator validates/corrects each output, then synthesizes. This is the best default when a task decomposes into parallel analysis pieces.

class Analyst(CentralizedAgentSystem):
    name = "analyst"
    system_prompt = "You are a careful financial analyst. Show assumptions."
    worker_count = 3
    max_subtasks = 3
    validate_outputs = True

docs.title: DecentralizedAgentSystem — peer debate
docs.text:
Peers answer, then read each other's answers for a bounded number of debate rounds, then synthesize. The paper found this useful for dynamic, high-entropy search such as web navigation.

class Scout(DecentralizedAgentSystem):
    name = "scout"
    system_prompt = "Explore widely, then reconcile conflicting findings."
    worker_count = 3
    debate_rounds = 1         # clamped to 0..3

docs.title: HybridAgentSystem — hierarchy + lateral review
docs.text:
Orchestrator decomposition and validation, followed by peer review rounds, then synthesis. Highest coordination cost (515% overhead in the paper). Reserve it for high-value tasks that need both structure and cross-checking.

class DeepReview(HybridAgentSystem):
    name = "deep-review"
    worker_count = 3
    debate_rounds = 1

docs.title: AdaptiveAgentSystem — select at run time
docs.text:
Supply a task profile in request.metadata["task_profile"] (or in the agent config). Without a profile it stays on the single-agent default.

class Router(AdaptiveAgentSystem):
    name = "router"
    system_prompt = "Answer the task using the selected coordination pattern."

router = Router(runtime, task_profile={
    "decomposability": 0.8,
    "sequential_dependencies": 0.1,
    "tool_count": 5,
    "single_agent_baseline": 0.35,
})

{"message": "Compare the three plans", "task_profile": {
  "decomposability": 0.8,
  "sequential_dependencies": 0.1,
  "tool_count": 5,
  "single_agent_baseline": 0.35
}}

recommend_architecture() can also be called directly:

from vira.agent import TaskProfile, recommend_architecture

rec = recommend_architecture(TaskProfile(
    decomposability=0.7,
    sequential_dependencies=0.2,
    tool_count=5,
    single_agent_baseline=0.35,
))
print(rec.architecture, rec.confidence, rec.reasons, rec.warnings)

docs.title: Selection rules
docs.text:
The implementation applies the paper's rules in this order:

  1. Sequential or non-decomposable (sequential_dependencies ≥ 0.6 or decomposability ≤ 0.35) → single.
  2. Tool-heavy (tool_count ≥ 12) → decentralized.
  3. Capability ceiling (single_agent_baseline ≥ 0.45) → single.
  4. Dynamic environment with decomposable work → decentralized.
  5. Needs peer review with decomposable work → hybrid.
  6. Decomposable analysis (decomposability ≥ 0.55) → centralized.
  7. Otherwise → single (conservative fallback).

Profiles are clamped to [0, 1], and worker/round limits are bounded so a misconfiguration cannot fan out without limit.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Authenticated clients can inspect the catalog and ask for a recommendation:

curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-architectures \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-architectures/recommend \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"decomposability": 0.8, "sequential_dependencies": 0.1,
       "tool_count": 5, "single_agent_baseline": 0.35}'

The response includes the chosen topology, confidence, reasons, warnings and the measured coordination profile.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Register an architecture class exactly like any other agent:

agents:
  - name: Analyst
    module: my_package.agents
    class: Analyst
    enabled: true
    config:
      worker_count: 3
      max_subtasks: 3
      debate_rounds: 1
      validate_outputs: true
      max_seconds: 240
      tools:
        allow: ["knowledge_search", "database_query"]

Useful config keys:

Key Default Meaning worker_count 3 Parallel workers/peers, clamped to 1–8. max_subtasks worker_count Maximum planner subtasks. debate_rounds 1 Peer-review rounds, clamped to 0–3. validate_outputs true Centralized/hybrid validation pass. architecture_timeout max_seconds Per-LLM-call timeout. worker_max_tokens derived Optional explicit worker token budget. worker_prompt / synthesis_prompt / orchestrator_prompt / validation_prompt / debate_prompt built in Override prompt templates.

The worker budget is derived from the agent's max_tokens so the total multi-agent budget stays close to the single-agent budget.

docs.title: Observability and safety
docs.text:
Each run records architecture and a coordination block in TaskResult.data:

{
  "architecture": "centralized",
  "coordination": {
    "workers": 3,
    "rounds": 1,
    "subtasks": ["revenue", "costs", "risks"],
    "validated": true,
    "corrections": 1,
    "llm_calls": 8,
    "profile": {"overhead_pct": 285, "error_amplification": 4.4}
  }
}

Timeline events (architecture.start, architecture.plan, architecture.llm, architecture.debate) appear in the run trace. AgentMetadata.architecture and BaseAgent.describe() expose the chosen topology to the registry and dashboard.

Guidelines:

  • Start with SingleAgent. Only move up when the task profile justifies it.
  • Do not use multi-agent coordination for sequential planning or a small tool count with a strong single-agent baseline.
  • Treat IndependentAgentSystem as an ensemble, not an accuracy guarantee.
  • Keep worker_count, debate_rounds and max_seconds small on local models.
  • The multi-agent classes do not add tool loops to workers by default. Override _llm or _run_workers if you need tool-using workers; remember the paper's tool-coordination trade-off.

docs.title: VIRA agent design (v2)
docs.text:
Agent code is split into three layers. Developers should only need the top layer for most agents and the middle layer for LLM/tool agents.

Layer File Responsibility BaseAgent vira/agent/base.py lifecycle, task contract, per-task identity, tool/memory/knowledge/progress/response helpers, safe concurrency LLMAgent vira/agent/llm_agent.py prompt construction, tool selection, multi-step loop, retry, specialist delegation, lesson learning ChatAgent vira/agent/Agents/chat_agent.py chat event mapping, conversation history, agent.response emission

Supporting pieces:

Piece File What it does Agent loop vira/agent/loop.py think -> one tool call -> observe -> repeat, with a step budget, repeat/unknown-tool guards, errors fed back for self-correction, forced final answer, context compaction. Any permitted tool can now be called by name even if it was not in the small prompt selection Tool policy + discovery vira/agent/toolbox.py allow/deny/pinned globs, local and qualified MCP tools, catalog selection, correct permission action per tool Tolerant parsing vira/agent/toolcalls.py accepts fenced/quoted/trailing-comma JSON and common key variants, so 3B-8B models rarely break the protocol Sub-agents vira/agent/definitions/*.md one markdown file per specialist (frontmatter: name, description, tools, max_steps). Delegation runs a fresh, small context Self-improvement vira/agent/lessons.py failed/recovered tool calls become per-user lesson memories, recalled into the next prompt. No extra LLM call

docs.title: Write a task agent
docs.text:
from vira.agent import BaseAgent


class InboxAgent(BaseAgent):
    name = "inbox"
    role = "inbox"                 # stable knowledge scope, not the runtime id

    async def setup(self):
        self._seen = set()

    async def execute(self, request):
        # request.message / request.input / request.user_id / request.run_id
        self.emit_progress("status", label="Reading inbox")
        items = await self.call_tool("database_query", query="select * from ...")
        return {"response": f"found {len(items)} items"}

run_task/handle normalise the return value into a TaskResult, attach identity in context variables (so concurrent users never leak into each other) and run the error hook on failure.

docs.title: Chat-facing agents
docs.text:
ConversationalAgent owns the user.message -> agent.response protocol, history fallback and routing. Subclass it for a chat-selectable specialist:

class MyChatAgent(ConversationalAgent):
    role = "my-specialist"
    is_default_agent = False       # only answers an explicit agent_id
    default_system_prompt = "..."

The API includes agent_id in the event and validates it; without a target, only the default ChatAgent answers. This prevents duplicate replies when several chat agents are registered.

docs.title: Shipped agent
docs.text:
Agent Selection Purpose ChatAgent default, agent_id: chatbot general assistant

Everything else is an extension point: create a BaseAgent/LLMAgent/ ConversationalAgent subclass and register it in config.yaml. Tools are general capabilities granted through tools.allow; there are no per-agent private tools.

docs.title: Workspaces and host tools
docs.text:
The durable unit is a user-visible workspace; agent sandboxes attach to it. All agents for a user share the default workspace, and several agents can attach to the same project without sharing a process namespace. A chat request may pass workspace: "<name-or-absolute-path>", which is injected into every sandbox tool call for that run.

Host-installed tools are available in two ways:

  • workspace.default_execution_mode: host (or per-workspace execution_mode) runs commands in the workspace with the host PATH;
  • sandbox.readonly_mounts + sandbox.extra_path keep bubblewrap isolation and expose host tool directories read-only.

See docs/dev/designs/workspaces.md.

docs.title: Write an LLM agent
docs.text:
from vira.agent import LLMAgent


class Researcher(LLMAgent):
    role = "researcher"

    def __init__(self, runtime, **config):
        config.setdefault("system_prompt", "Research carefully and cite sources.")
        config.setdefault("tools", {"allow": ["web", "web_*", "rag_search"]})
        super().__init__(runtime, **config)

Set delegation: true to expose markdown specialists as a delegate tool.

docs.title: Helpers available on every agent
docs.text: Helper Purpose call_llm / ask_llm LLM call with task identity and usage accounting call_tool Execute a tool with the declared permission action; injects the caller for local tools and only declared args for MCP tools recall / remember Episodic memory knowledge_search / knowledge_write Scoped knowledge base emit_progress Streaming + durable run timeline respond Emit the agent's response event to the requesting user send_event Message another agent

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• There is exactly one shipped chat agent: ChatAgent, connected to the chat webpage. Every other agent is written by extending BaseAgent (or LLMAgent) and registering it in config.yaml.
  • execute is the single required method. initialize rejects a class that does not implement it, so a half-written agent fails at startup instead of silently doing nothing.
  • Choose a coordination topology from vira/agent/architectures.py: SingleAgent (default), IndependentAgentSystem, CentralizedAgentSystem, DecentralizedAgentSystem, HybridAgentSystem or AdaptiveAgentSystem. The selection rules and the evidence behind them are in Agent architectures.
  • There is one BaseAgent implementation. The old orchestration copy and the example/sensor agents were removed; scheduler, router, workflows and plugins all use vira.agent.base.BaseAgent.
  • ChatAgent keeps its public config (tools.allow/deny/pinned, tool_timeouts, delegation, history_limit) and its user.message -> agent.response contract.

Tuning for small contexts: lower max_prompt_chars, max_tool_chars, max_steps in config.yaml.

docs.title: Database tools (read-only)
docs.text:
VIRA ships a dedicated MCP server at vira/tools/database_mcp_server.py. It lets the Chatbot and agents inspect the server database safely, without giving them write access.

The server is enabled by default in config.yaml:

database_mcp:
  enabled: true
  permissions: ["read", "execute"]

The orchestrator connects it at boot and registers the tools under the database_query namespace.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Purpose database_query.database_tables List queryable tables, descriptions and key columns. database_query.database_schema Show full columns, types and foreign keys for matching tables. database_query.database_examples Curated SQL templates for common questions. database_query.database_account_summary Safe summary of the signed-in user's own account. database_query.database_query Run one custom SELECT/WITH query (administrators).

The intended workflow for the model is:

database_tables -> database_schema -> database_query

Example questions and queries:

-- Devices connected with the signed-in account
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT d.id) AS devices
FROM devices d
JOIN user_device_access a ON a.device_id = d.id
WHERE a.user_id = {{caller_user_id}}
  AND a.status = 'active'
  AND d.status = 'active';

-- Devices connected with the server
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM devices
GROUP BY status;

{{caller_user_id}} is replaced by the authenticated caller's user id. The agent loop injects that identity only for the database_query.* tools; the model never needs to guess or type another user's id.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Read-only connection: SQLite is opened with mode=ro and PRAGMA query_only = ON; PostgreSQL sessions use default_transaction_read_only.
  • One statement only: SELECT and WITH are allowed. Multiple statements and comments that hide additional statements are rejected.
  • Writes blocked: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, PRAGMA, ATTACH, VACUUM, GRANT, COPY and similar keywords are rejected before execution.
  • Secret columns and tables hidden: password hashes, recovery codes, session hashes, credential hashes, tokens, vectors and internal tables are excluded from the schema and blocked in queries.
  • Row cap and timeout: at most 200 rows, with a short statement timeout.
  • Role gate: custom SQL requires an administrator account. Every user can call database_account_summary, which only returns their own aggregate information.
  • Every call still goes through the normal tool permission and audit path.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_database_query -v

The tests cover schema filtering, write rejection, secret-column rejection, caller-scoped placeholders and the account summary.

docs.title: VIRA Framework — Developer Documentation
docs.text: Virtual Intelligent Runtime Agent framework An async, event-driven AI kernel for building context-aware autonomous agents.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Architecture Overview
  2. Boot Sequence
  3. Event Standard (Kernel Events)
  4. Agent Events
  5. Agent Specification
  6. Sensor Specification
  7. Memory Schema
  8. Workflow Schema
  9. Config Reference
  10. LLM Providers

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: For the target high-level and low-level design, persistence boundaries, database selection guidance, and migration plan, see SYSTEM_DESIGN.md.

docs.title: Boot Sequence
docs.text:
When python run.py is executed, the kernel boots in this exact order:

Step State What happens 1 LOADING_CONFIG ConfigManager reads config.yaml 2 STARTING_EVENT_BUS EventBus async queue initialised 3 SERVICE_REGISTRY Core services registered by name 4 STARTING_STATE_MANAGER Checkpoint directory prepared 5 STARTING_SCHEDULER Tick loop started 6 LOADING_CORE_MODULES Modules in vira/modules/core/ loaded and started 7 LOADING_PLUGINS Plugin directory scanned 8 STARTING_SENSORS Enabled sensors in config.yaml instantiated and started 9 RUNNING kernel.ready event published; API server starts

docs.title: Event Standard (Kernel Events)
docs.text: All events in VIRA share a single structure, defined in vira/kernel/event_bus.py.

docs.title: Event dataclass
docs.text:
@dataclass
class Event:
    type: str                          # dot-namespaced string, e.g. "sensor.hardware.state"
    data: Any                          # dict payload — structure depends on event type
    source: str = "kernel"             # component that created the event
    kind: EventKind = DOMAIN           # DOMAIN | COMMAND | SYSTEM
    priority: EventPriority = NORMAL   # LOW | NORMAL | HIGH | CRITICAL
    event_id: str = uuid4()            # stable identity for retries/idempotency
    correlation_id: str = uuid4()      # links related events across the system
    causation_id: Optional[str]        # event that caused this event
    timestamp: float = time.time()     # Unix timestamp (seconds)
    durable: bool = False              # persist through the SQLite outbox
    verified: bool = False             # set True by EventDispatcher on security pass

docs.title: Event naming convention
docs.text:
Events follow a domain.entity.action pattern:

Namespace Examples Emitted by sensor.* sensor.hardware.state, sensor.system.state Sensors kernel.* kernel.ready, kernel.shutdown Kernel agent.* agent.registered, agent.unregistered AgentManager user.* user.message, user.activity User-activity sensor / API fs.* fs.file.created, fs.file.modified, fs.file.deleted FileSystemSensor workflow.* workflow.started, workflow.completed, workflow.failed WorkflowEngine memory.* memory.stored, memory.retrieved MemoryManager tool.* tool.invoked, tool.result ToolExecutor

docs.title: Priority levels
docs.text: EventPriority Value When to use LOW 0 Background metrics, periodic logs NORMAL 1 Default for all sensor readings HIGH 2 User-triggered actions CRITICAL 3 Security violations, kernel errors, OOM signals

docs.title: Publishing an event
docs.text:
# Via EventDispatcher (recommended — applies security + pipeline)
await dispatcher.publish(Event(
    type="user.message",
    data={"text": "Hello", "session_id": "abc123"},
    source="api",
    priority=EventPriority.HIGH
))

# Convenience dict form
await dispatcher.publish_dict("sensor.cpu.spike", {"cpu_pct": 92.4}, source="hardware_sensor")

Durable state changes set durable=True. The dispatcher records those events in the SQLite outbox before delivery. The kernel retries pending outbox rows after restart. High-frequency sensor telemetry remains non-durable by default. Commands use kind=EventKind.COMMAND and are checked against command permissions before they are accepted.

Consumers that update durable state should use vira.kernel.handle_idempotently so a retried event is applied once per consumer. Operational status is available from /health, /metrics, /ops/sensors, and /ops/events/lag.

docs.title: Agents and tools
docs.text:
Agents are registered with versioned metadata independent of their in-memory instances. Capabilities carry input and output schemas, and subscribed event types determine routing. Agent definitions are stored in SQLite and can be enabled, disabled, or unregistered through the authenticated /agents API.

Agent modules must match agent_policy.allowed_modules in config.yaml. Only agents listed in the startup agents: configuration are loaded by default. Persisted agent definitions from the authenticated dashboard/database are ignored at boot unless agent_policy.load_persisted_agents: true is explicitly configured. This prevents a previously enabled agent from restarting after it is removed or disabled in config.yaml. This allow-list is enforced before importing a configured agent module.

Tool execution goes through ToolExecutor, which checks both the tool's declared actions and the central security manager before execution. Every attempt is recorded in SQLite with the request, result, status, permission decision, duration, agent ID, and correlation ID. Recent records are available from /tools/calls.

docs.title: Conversations, runs, memory, and context
docs.text:
Conversations, messages, and agent runs are persisted in SQLite and scoped to the authenticated user. Message creation accepts an Idempotency-Key, keeps sequence ordering, correlation IDs, and run IDs, and exposes paginated history through /conversations/{conversation_id}/messages. The /chat endpoint creates a queued run, uses bounded persisted history, and records the assistant message and final run status.

Memory is stored with user, agent, conversation, type, metadata, importance, and expiry scope. Use /memories for explicit storage, filtered search, and deletion. MemoryManager provides the same scoped operations to agents. ContextManager.assemble_context bounds messages and memories before they are sent to an LLM.

docs.title: Subscribing to events
docs.text:
# Subscribe to a specific event type
event_bus.subscribe("sensor.hardware.state", my_async_callback)

# Subscribe to all events (wildcard)
event_bus.subscribe_all(debug_logger)

docs.title: Agent Events
docs.text: Defined in vira/agent_orchestration/events.py. These Pydantic models are used for inter-agent and orchestration-level signalling.

docs.title: AgentEvent
docs.text:
class AgentEvent(BaseModel):
    agent_id: str        # UUID of the source agent
    event_type: str      # mirrors kernel event type namespace
    data: Dict           # arbitrary payload

docs.title: TaskEvent
docs.text:
class TaskEvent(BaseModel):
    task_id: str                    # UUID
    workflow_id: str                # UUID of the parent workflow
    step_id: str                    # ID of the workflow step
    status: str                     # "pending" | "running" | "completed" | "failed" | "cancelled"
    result: Optional[Any] = None    # step output on success
    error: Optional[str] = None     # error message on failure

docs.text:
class MemoryEvent(BaseModel):
    operation: str                    # "store" | "retrieve" | "delete"
    agent_id: str                     # which agent performed the operation
    memory_id: Optional[str] = None   # UUID of the memory entry

docs.title: AgentMessage (inter-agent messaging via AgentMessageBus)
docs.text:
Defined in vira/agent_orchestration/messages.py and delivered by vira/agent_orchestration/message_bus.py:

class AgentMessage(BaseModel):
    type: str                                  # event type (matches kernel Event)
    data: Any                                  # arbitrary payload
    sender_agent_id: Optional[str] = None      # None = external/kernel event
    target_agent_ids: Optional[List[str]] = None
    exclude_sender: bool = True
    event_id: Optional[str] = None
    correlation_id: Optional[str] = None
    device_id: Optional[str] = None
    actor_user_id: Optional[int] = None
    source_component: Optional[str] = None

Subscribe with await bus.subscribe(event_type, callback) and remove the same callback with await bus.unsubscribe(event_type, callback); "*" subscribes to every message type.

docs.title: Agent Specification
docs.text:
Agents extend BaseAgent (vira/agent/base.py) and implement execute. The old think/plan/act/reflect pipeline was removed; those names remain only as non-required compatibility hooks and must not be used for new agents.

For multi-agent coordination, extend one of the architecture bases in vira/agent/architectures.py (SingleAgent, IndependentAgentSystem, CentralizedAgentSystem, DecentralizedAgentSystem, HybridAgentSystem, or the runtime selector AdaptiveAgentSystem). See Agent architectures.

docs.title: Required interface
docs.text:
from vira.agent import BaseAgent
from vira.agent_orchestration.registry import AgentCapability


class MyAgent(BaseAgent):
    name = "MyAgent"
    role = "my-agent"                 # stable knowledge scope, not the runtime id

    def __init__(self, runtime, **config):
        super().__init__(
            name=self.name,
            description="What this agent does in one sentence.",
            runtime=runtime,
            **config,
        )
        self._capabilities = [
            AgentCapability(
                name="do_something",
                description="Does the thing",
                input_schema={"text": "str"},     # optional JSON schema dict
                output_schema={"result": "str"},
            )
        ]
        # Declare which kernel events this agent handles
        self._subscribed_events = ["user.message", "sensor.hardware.state"]
        # Optional: run on an interval (seconds), set to None for event-only
        self._interval_seconds = None

    # ---- Mandatory method ----

    async def execute(self, request):
        """Handle one TaskRequest. Return a string, dict or TaskResult."""
        result = await self.call_tool("some_tool", text=request.message)
        return {"response": result}

initialize() rejects classes that do not override execute. run_task adds lifecycle and error handling, per-task identity and return-value normalisation; raise an exception to record a failed task, or return a TaskResult for control over the error and duration fields.

docs.title: Task contract
docs.text:
@dataclass
class TaskRequest:
    input: Any = None
    event: Any = None
    user_id: Optional[int] = None
    organization_id: Optional[str] = None
    conversation_id: Optional[str] = None
    device_id: Optional[str] = None
    run_id: Optional[str] = None
    history: List[Dict[str, Any]] = ...
    metadata: Dict[str, Any] = ...
    timeout: Optional[float] = None
    context: Any = None

@dataclass
class TaskResult:
    text: str = ""
    data: Dict[str, Any] = ...
    steps: List[Any] = ...
    tool_calls: int = 0
    stopped: str = "final"
    error: Optional[str] = None
    duration_ms: float = 0.0
    raw: Any = None

request.message returns the text from a dict input (message/text), or the plain string input.

docs.title: Lifecycle hooks (optional)
docs.text: setup(), on_start(), on_stop(), on_error(request, error), before_run(request) and after_run(request, result).

docs.title: Agent lifecycle states
docs.text:
INITIALIZED → READY → RUNNING → READY
                              ↘ FAILED
                    → WAITING
                    → TERMINATED

docs.title: Registering an agent in config.yaml
docs.text:
agents:
  - name: MyAgent
    module: my_package.my_agent       # Python import path
    class: MyAgent                    # Class name inside the module
    enabled: true
    config:
      some_param: value               # passed to the agent constructor
    subscribed_events:
      - "user.message"

docs.text:
await self.send_event(
    event_type="agent.my_agent.result",
    data={"output": result},
    target_agent_ids=None            # None = broadcast; list of IDs = targeted
)

docs.title: Sensor Specification
docs.text: All sensors extend BaseSensor (vira/sensors/base_sensor.py).

docs.title: Required interface
docs.text:
class MySensor(BaseSensor):
    def __init__(self, interval: float, event_bus: EventBus, dispatcher: EventDispatcher):
        super().__init__(name="my_sensor")
        self._interval = interval
        self._event_bus = event_bus
        self._dispatcher = dispatcher

    async def start(self) -> None:
        """Start the polling loop."""
        self._running = True
        asyncio.create_task(self._poll())

    async def stop(self) -> None:
        self._running = False

    async def read(self):
        """Read raw sensor data. Return a dict."""
        return {"value": 42}

    async def _poll(self):
        while self._running:
            data = await self.read()
            await self._dispatcher.publish(Event(
                type="sensor.my_sensor.state",
                data=data,
                source=self.name
            ))
            await asyncio.sleep(self._interval)

docs.title: Registering a custom sensor
docs.text:
# In your own code (before kernel.boot())
from vira.kernel.kernel import Kernel

Kernel.register_sensor("my_sensor", lambda cfg, eb, disp, mm: MySensor(
    interval=cfg.get("interval", 5.0),
    event_bus=eb,
    dispatcher=disp
))

Then enable it in config.yaml:

sensors:
  - name: my_sensor
    enabled: true
    interval: 5.0

docs.title: Memory Schema
docs.text:
The in-process item contract is MemoryItem in vira/memory/base.py; persistent memories are stored and scoped by vira/auth/database.py (user, agent, conversation, type, importance, expiry).

class MemoryItem(BaseModel):
    id: str                            # UUID
    content: str                       # text content of the memory
    embedding: Optional[List[float]]   # vector embedding for similarity search
    metadata: Dict[str, Any]           # tags, source, scope identifiers
    timestamp: datetime
    ttl: Optional[int]                 # seconds; None = no expiry

docs.title: Memory types
docs.text: Type Lifetime Use case short_term Minutes–hours Current task context, recent messages long_term Indefinite User preferences, learned patterns episodic Indefinite Records of past events and agent actions semantic Indefinite Facts, domain knowledge, distilled understanding

docs.title: Workflow Schema
docs.text:
Defined in vira/agent_orchestration/workflow.py:

class WorkflowStep(BaseModel):
    id: str                            # unique step identifier
    name: str                          # human-readable label
    agent_id: str                      # which registered agent to invoke
    input: Dict[str, Any] = {}         # static input; supports {{ context.key }} and {{ results.step_id }} placeholders
    depends_on: List[str] = []         # step IDs that must complete first (DAG edges)
    retry_policy: Optional[Dict] = None  # {"max_retries": 3, "delay": 1}
    compensation: Optional[str] = None  # step ID to invoke on failure (saga pattern)

class Workflow(BaseModel):
    id: str
    name: str
    steps: List[WorkflowStep]
    status: WorkflowStatus             # pending | running | completed | failed | cancelled
    context: Dict[str, Any] = {}       # shared context across all steps
    created_at: float
    completed_at: Optional[float]

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text:
from vira.agent_orchestration.workflow import Workflow, WorkflowStep

wf = Workflow(
    id="wf-001",
    name="file_analysis",
    context={"target_path": "/home/user/docs"},
    steps=[
        WorkflowStep(id="scan", name="Scan files", agent_id="scanner_agent_id"),
        WorkflowStep(
            id="summarize",
            name="Summarise findings",
            agent_id="summarizer_agent_id",
            depends_on=["scan"],
            input={"scan_result": "{{ results.scan }}"}
        ),
    ]
)

await workflow_engine.execute(wf)

docs.title: Config Reference
docs.text:
Full config.yaml key reference:

kernel:
  name: VIRA
  checkpoint_dir: ./data/checkpoints    # StateManager save location
  logs_dir: ./data/logs
  plugins_dir: ./vira/plugins           # scanned for plugin classes
  modules_dir: ./vira/modules/core      # scanned for module classes

auth:
  secret_key: "CHANGE_ME"              # random secret for session tokens
  session_cookie_name: "vira_session"
  session_max_age: 86400               # seconds (24h)
  database_url: "sqlite:///data/vira.sqlite3"

event_bus:
  max_queue_size: 10000                # async queue capacity

scheduler:
  tick_interval: 1.0                   # seconds between scheduler ticks

security:
  default_permissions:                 # granted to all sources by default
    - "event.publish.*"
    - "context.read"
    - "context.write"
    - "memory.store.*"
    - "memory.get.*"
    - "llm.call.*"

metrics:
  enabled: true
  retention_minutes: 60

sensors:                               # list of sensor configs
  - name: wayland_idle_sensor          # must match a registered factory name
    enabled: true
    interval: 5.0                      # polling interval in seconds

llm:
  default_model: "qwen3.5:9b"       # VIRA's final default local model choice
  models:
    - name: "local-llama"
      provider: "ollama"               # "ollama" | "openai" | "anthropic"
      model: "qwen3.5:9b"
      base_url: "http://localhost:11434"
      temperature: 0.8
      num_ctx: 16384
    - name: "gpt-4"
      provider: "openai"
      api_key: "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"     # resolved from env
      model: "gpt-4"
      max_tokens: 4096
      temperature: 0.7

agents:                                # auto-loaded agents
  - name: MyAgent
    module: my_package.my_agent
    class: MyAgent
    enabled: true
    config: {}
    subscribed_events: []

mcp_server:
  command: ["python", "vira/tools/mcp_server.py"]
  permissions: ["read", "write", "execute"]

docs.title: LLM Providers
docs.text:
VIRA supports three LLM backends via vira/llm/:

Provider Class Config key Auth Ollama (local) OllamaLLM provider: "ollama" None — local HTTP OpenAI OpenAILLM provider: "openai" api_key in config or $OPENAI_API_KEY Anthropic AnthropicLLM provider: "anthropic" api_key in config or $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

VIRA ships configured for qwen3.5:9b through Ollama. This is the final default model choice for the framework; install it with ollama pull qwen3.5:9b. Other providers and models remain fully supported and can be selected explicitly.

The LLMManager selects the backend at runtime via LLMFactory. Agents call:

response = await self.runtime.call_llm(self.agent_id, prompt)

The runtime resolves which model to use from the agent's config or falls back to llm.default_model in config.yaml.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the target architecture for VIRA. It focuses on users, conversations, agents, workflows, memory, events and database selection. The design keeps VIRA as a modular monolith first and allows individual runtime components to scale independently later.

docs.title: Current implementation summary
docs.text:
VIRA is an asynchronous Python application composed of:

  • FastAPI HTTP routes in vira/api/app.py
  • Kernel lifecycle and event processing in vira/kernel/
  • Agents and lifecycle contracts in vira/agent/
  • Agent routing and scheduling in vira/agent_orchestration/
  • LLM and tool access through vira/agent_runtime/
  • Authentication and SQLite access in vira/auth/
  • SQLite-backed conversations, messages, agent runs, scoped memories, agent definitions, tool-call audits, and outbox events

The current system persists users, hashed sessions, roles, authentication audit events, conversations, ordered messages, run status, scoped memories, agent definitions, and tool-call records. Chat execution still uses the in-process event bus and configured agent runtime, while durable records provide restart survival and ownership enforcement.

docs.title: 1.1 Identity and access
docs.text: ID Requirement Priority FR-01 A user can create the initial administrator account. Must FR-02 A user can log in and log out. Must FR-03 A user can reset a password using a recovery code. Must FR-04 Every authenticated request has a typed principal containing user_id, roles, and session ID. Must FR-05 Users can only access their own conversations, runs, memories, and agents unless explicitly shared. Must FR-06 Sessions can expire and be revoked. Should FR-07 Authentication and authorization decisions are auditable. Should

docs.text: ID Requirement Priority FR-08 A user can create, list, rename, archive, and delete conversations. Must FR-09 A user can append messages to a conversation. Must FR-10 Messages preserve role, ordering, timestamps, correlation ID, and optional run ID. Must FR-11 Chat history survives process restarts. Must FR-12 Chat history is paginated and bounded before being sent to an LLM. Must FR-13 A message submission is idempotent using a client idempotency key. Must FR-14 The user can observe run status and receive assistant responses through polling or streaming. Must FR-15 The system can retain system, assistant, user, and tool messages. Should

Must FR-17 Agent definitions are versioned and persisted independently from loaded Python instances. Must FR-18 Agents expose capabilities, input schemas, output schemas, and subscribed events. Must FR-19 The system can enable, disable, register, and unregister agents. Must FR-20 Tool calls are permission checked before execution. Must FR-21 Every tool call records request, result, status, permission decision, and duration. Must FR-22 User-created agent modules are allow-listed and run with restricted permissions. Must

Must FR-25 A run records individual think, plan, LLM, tool, and reflect steps. Must FR-26 Worker failure does not silently lose a run. Must FR-27 Stale running jobs can be retried or marked failed. Must FR-28 Workflows can execute ordered or DAG-based agent steps. Should FR-29 Run cancellation is propagated to the scheduler and active tools where possible. Should

docs.text: ID Requirement Priority FR-30 Agents can store, retrieve, delete, and compact memory. Must FR-31 Memory is scoped by user, agent, conversation, and memory type. Must FR-32 Memory supports metadata filtering and optional semantic similarity search. Should FR-33 Memory supports expiry and retention policies. Should FR-34 Context assembly returns a bounded, relevant prompt context. Must

docs.title: 1.6 Kernel, events, sensors, and operations
docs.text: ID Requirement Priority FR-35 Sensors publish typed events through the kernel dispatcher. Must FR-36 Commands and domain events are distinguishable. Must FR-37 Durable state changes produce outbox events. Must FR-38 Event consumers are idempotent and retryable. Must FR-39 Operators can inspect health, metrics, active agents, event lag, and failed runs. Must FR-40 Large results and artifacts can be stored outside transactional rows. Should

docs.title: 2.1 Quality attributes
docs.text: Attribute Requirement and target Availability Local mode should recover after restart. Production mode should avoid single-process state for durable data. Durability Committed users, messages, runs, tool calls, and audit records must survive process failure. Consistency Ownership checks, message ordering, and run state transitions must be transactional. Performance Conversation list/history reads should normally complete under 200 ms at the service layer; chat generation is asynchronous. Throughput The system must support batched append-only writes for messages, steps, tool calls, and outbox events. Scalability API and worker processes can be separated without changing domain services. Recovery Queued jobs can be reclaimed; failed events can be retried or dead-lettered. Security Deny-by-default tool permissions, hashed passwords/tokens, tenant isolation, redacted logs. Privacy Local deployments must not send data anywhere except explicitly configured LLM/tool providers. Extensibility Database, event transport, LLM provider, vector store, and object store are adapters behind ports. Observability Correlation IDs connect HTTP requests, events, runs, steps, LLM calls, and tools. Maintainability API routes contain transport logic only; application services contain use cases; repositories contain persistence. Testability Domain/application services can be tested with fake repositories and event publishers. Portability SQLite is supported for single-user local mode; PostgreSQL is supported for multi-process production mode.

docs.title: 2.2 Capacity assumptions
docs.text:
The initial design assumes:

  • Tens of thousands of messages per user, not unlimited transcript growth.
  • Hundreds of registered agents and tools per installation.
  • Up to tens of concurrent agent runs in a single local process.
  • Sensor telemetry is sampled or aggregated before durable storage.
  • Large files, screenshots, and raw tool output are not stored in message rows.

When these assumptions are exceeded, use the scaling options in Section 3.5 and Section 5.
