docs.title: 8.2 Component responsibilities
docs.text:
• Endpoint client/agent: gathers only platform-permitted capabilities, sends heartbeats and bounded event batches, handles retries, maintains a per-device sequence when feasible, and stores credentials in OS-secure storage. It does not decide the authoritative user/device identity.
  • API gateway: versioning, request validation, rate limiting, error mapping, correlation IDs, and transport-specific concerns. It contains no business persistence rules.
  • Authentication: resolves user sessions, device credentials, and service identities into different typed principals.
  • Authorization: verifies role plus resource ownership/access on every request and stream subscription.
  • Device service: registration, capabilities, status, access grants, credential rotation, and revocation.
  • Event ingestion service: validates type/schema/size, resolves provenance, deduplicates, persists durable events, and writes outbox rows transactionally.
  • Application services: users, conversations, messages, runs, memories, agents, and tools.
  • Kernel/event adapters: route normalized events to local subscribers or a durable broker. A local in-process bus is an adapter, not the multi-process source of truth.
  • Repositories/migrations: own SQL and constraints; provide SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters where required.
  • Operations service: metrics, event lag, device health, failed deliveries, and admin audit views with access filtering.

docs.title: 8.3 Deployment modes
docs.text:
Local development: FastAPI + kernel/worker in one process, SQLite WAL, local event bus, local artifact storage. The same device and user contracts are enforced even when server and client run on the same computer.

Multi-user production: FastAPI/API processes + worker processes, PostgreSQL system of record, transactional outbox, durable broker/stream where cross-process delivery is needed, metrics/time-series storage only when justified, TLS termination, backups, and explicit credential/secret configuration.

Do not require a microservice split to achieve multi-device support. Start with a modular monolith and extract independently scalable components only when load and operational needs justify it.

docs.title: 9.1 Proposed package boundaries
docs.text:
vira/
  domain/
    identity.py             # UserPrincipal, DevicePrincipal, ServicePrincipal
    device.py               # Device, DeviceCredential, UserDeviceAccess
    event.py                # normalized EventEnvelope and schema metadata
  application/
    users/                  # create, list, deactivate, delete users
    devices/                # register, heartbeat, grant, revoke, rotate
    events/                 # ingest batch, dedupe, authorize, dispatch
    conversations/          # existing chat use cases
    ports.py                # repository and publisher protocols
  api/
    routes/
      auth.py
      admin_users.py
      devices.py
      device_events.py
      conversations.py
      operations.py
    dependencies.py         # typed principal and resource authorization
  infrastructure/
    persistence/
      migrations/
      sqlite/
      postgres/
      repositories.py
    events/
      local_bus.py
      outbox_publisher.py
      broker_adapter.py     # optional production adapter
  clients/
    contract/               # shared schema examples and conformance tests

This is a target structure, not a requirement to relocate every existing Python module in the first commit. Existing vira/auth, vira/kernel, and vira/api can be adapted incrementally while preserving their public contracts behind application services.

docs.title: 9.2 Ingest transaction and idempotency
docs.text:
For each batch:

  1. Authenticate the device credential and resolve its device_id, state, and scopes.
  2. Confirm the path device ID matches the credential's device ID and that the device is active.
  3. Validate batch size, event schema, payload size, timestamp, event type allow-list, and supported schema version.
  4. For each item, compute/verify a canonical payload hash and attempt to insert by unique event_id.
  5. If the ID already exists with the same hash, report it as a duplicate and do not repeat side effects. If the same ID has a different hash, return a conflict and record a security diagnostic.
  6. For durable event types, insert the normalized event row and its outbox record in the same transaction.
  7. Commit before acknowledging acceptance. Return item-level results.
  8. The outbox publisher retries transient failures with bounded backoff; consumers record (consumer_name, event_id) after successful handling.
  9. Update device heartbeat/last-seen independently of whether a specific event is a duplicate, provided the authenticated request is valid.

Acknowledge at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, not an unsupported promise of exactly-once delivery across a network. Event occurrence time is not a strict global ordering guarantee; use device sequence and receipt time to diagnose reordering.

docs.title: 9.3 Authorization rules
docs.text:
• admin: manage accounts and installation operations; device visibility is explicit unless the operations policy grants fleet-wide access.
  • user: access owned resources and devices granted through user_device_access.
  • device: write only to device-scoped endpoints permitted by credential scopes; cannot call user/admin routes.
  • service: narrowly scoped internal permissions; no use of a human session cookie.
  • User–device access roles: owner can manage grants and revoke; operator can use permitted capabilities; viewer can inspect allowed status/events. Exact capability actions are policy-controlled.
  • Every repository operation accepting a user-scoped resource must include ownership/access predicates. Never fetch by ID and rely on the UI to hide unauthorized records.
  • Event stream subscriptions must apply the same ACL as event list APIs. Never broadcast all events to every authenticated SSE queue.

docs.title: 9.4 State machines
docs.text:
Device: pending → active → revoked → retired; revocation is terminal for that credential. Re-enrollment creates or explicitly reactivates a device according to policy; it must not silently restore a leaked credential.

User: invited/pending → active → disabled → deleted; disabled users cannot create sessions. Deletion policy must specify what happens to conversations, memories, events, audit records, and ownership. Prefer deactivation/tombstone first, followed by an explicit retention/deletion workflow.

Event delivery: received → persisted → pending_dispatch → published; failed publication goes through bounded retry and then dead_letter. Duplicate receipt does not create a second durable event.

docs.title: 9.5 Error and retry rules
docs.text:
• 401: missing, invalid, expired, or revoked credential.
  • 403: valid principal but insufficient scope/role.
  • 404: unknown resource or concealed inaccessible resource.
  • 409: event ID reused with different payload, invalid state transition, or conflicting enrollment.
  • 413: request or batch exceeds configured payload limit.
  • 422: invalid event shape/schema/version.
  • 429: device/user rate limit exceeded; include retry guidance when safe.
  • 5xx: transient server-side failure; client retries with jitter and stable event IDs.

Never return credential hashes, raw tokens, password hashes, private sensor content, or unredacted tool/LLM secrets in errors or audit logs.

docs.title: 10. Requirement-to-Design Traceability
docs.text:
Requirement family API contract Entities HLD component LLD implementation Essential tests FR-ID-01–07 /auth/*, /admin/users/* users, user_sessions, auth_audit Authentication, Authorization, Admin API UserAdminService, auth dependencies, repositories bootstrap-once, last-admin protection, disabled/revoked session, audit records FR-DEV-01–08 /devices*, /devices/{id}/access* devices, device_credentials, user_device_access Device service, API, Authorization DeviceService, credential repository, migration multiple devices/user, shared grant, revocation, unsupported capability FR-EVT-01–10 /devices/{id}/events:batch, /events/stream device_events, outbox_events, event_consumptions Ingestion, dispatcher, operations EventIngestionService, publisher, event repository spoof rejection, idempotent retry, stream isolation, outbox recovery FR-APP-01–04 /conversations*, /runs*, /memories* current chat/runtime entities plus device FK on messages Application services, agent runtime existing repositories/services with access checks regression, user isolation, correct submitting device NFR-SEC-* all protected APIs identity and audit entities AuthN/AuthZ typed principals, scopes, policy checks negative authorization and secret-leak tests NFR-DUR-01 / REL-01 device batch and durable mutation APIs event journal + outbox DB + outbox + worker transaction and idempotency logic restart, duplicate replay, transient broker failure NFR-PORT-01 / COMP-01 versioned device/event schemas devices, event schema version client adapters contract schema and conformance suite Android/iOS/desktop contract tests and compatibility tests

A requirement is not complete until it appears in the API contract, is supported by the schema, has an owning component, has a concrete LLD implementation, and has at least one acceptance test.

docs.title: 11. Security, Privacy, and Operations
docs.text:
• Separate user and device authentication schemes and scopes. A lost phone/laptop must be revocable without changing the user's password or logging out every other device.
  • Keep device credentials in OS-secure storage and use TLS for all remote connections.
  • Apply rate limits by user, device, and endpoint; cap batch count, payload size, and event types.
  • Record device-created-at and server-received-at timestamps; treat client clock and payload values as untrusted input.
  • Minimize sensitive payloads by default. Define per-event retention and export/deletion rules before collecting screen, application, file, or activity data.
  • Device admin APIs should expose metadata and health by default, not raw activity payloads. Raw event access needs an explicit permission and audit trail.
  • Add health fields: last_seen_at, latest client version, credential status, ingest error count, last accepted sequence, queue/backlog where reported, and capability health.
  • Ensure logs and dashboards scope data to authorized administrators/users and do not become a cross-user side channel.

docs.title: 12. Migration and Delivery Sequence
docs.text: This sequence intentionally follows dependency order. Do not implement endpoint clients before the server identity/event contracts are stable.

docs.title: Phase 0 — Requirements and baseline
docs.text:
1. Confirm user roles, sharing model, target platforms, event classes, retention, expected users/devices/events, and admin capabilities.
  2. Mark existing features as retained, changed, or deprecated.
  3. Freeze the FR/NFR IDs and acceptance criteria in this document.
  4. Add tests reproducing existing event-stream cross-user exposure and API authorization behavior before changing them.

docs.title: Phase 1 — API and entity contracts
docs.text:
1. Approve UserPrincipal, DevicePrincipal, and ServicePrincipal semantics.
  2. Approve device enrollment, user–device grant, credential rotation, revocation, heartbeat, and event-batch schemas.
  3. Approve the canonical event envelope and event type/schema version policy.
  4. Update ERD and SQL migration drafts; verify every API foreign key has a corresponding entity and every entity has an owner/use case.
  5. Generate/validate OpenAPI schemas and example payloads from the same Pydantic/API schema definitions where possible.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Persistence and identity
docs.text:
1. Add users.public_id, device, credential, access-grant, and event-provenance tables with reversible/forward-tested migrations.
  2. Add repository ports and SQLite implementation; add PostgreSQL implementation when production multi-process deployment is required.
  3. Implement admin user CRUD with soft-delete/deactivate policy, last-admin protection, and audit records.
  4. Implement distinct user/device authentication dependencies and credential revocation.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Event ingress and isolation
docs.text:
1. Implement device registration, heartbeat, access grants, and credential lifecycle.
  2. Implement versioned batch ingest, payload validation, deduplication, durable event records, and outbox.
  3. Fix event stream isolation and resource authorization before exposing remote endpoints.
  4. Add rate limits, payload caps, health metrics, and dead-letter visibility.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Endpoint clients
docs.text:
1. Build one reference client/SDK and a contract conformance suite.
  2. Implement platform adapters for Android/iOS/Windows/macOS/Linux according to actual OS permissions and capabilities.
  3. Add offline queueing and backoff without changing the server event contract.
  4. Validate per-device credential storage and remote revocation on each platform.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Production readiness
docs.text:
1. Run multi-user/multi-device authorization tests and sustained/peak load tests.
  2. Verify backup, restore, restart recovery, outbox retry, and database migration.
  3. Configure TLS, secure secret handling, retention, rate limits, and alerts.
  4. Update SYSTEM_DESIGN.md, VIRA_DOCS.md, diagrams, OpenAPI, and implementation-status claims to describe the same target and shipped behavior.

docs.title: 13. Definition of Done
docs.text:
• [ ] Requirements and provisional performance targets are approved.
  • [ ] API schemas and canonical event envelope are versioned and validated.
  • [ ] ERD and migrations cover every entity referenced by the API and HLD.
  • [ ] Multiple user accounts can coexist; only administrators can perform account administration.
  • [ ] One user can register multiple devices; device access can be granted/revoked independently.
  • [ ] Device credentials are distinct from user sessions, stored safely, scoped, rotatable, and revocable.
  • [ ] Every stored endpoint event has authenticated device provenance and source component metadata.
  • [ ] Human actor attribution is nullable and never trusted from an unauthenticated payload field.
  • [ ] Replaying an event is safe; conflicting reuse of an event ID is rejected and audited.
  • [ ] Event streams and APIs cannot disclose another user's or device's data.
  • [ ] Existing chat, runs, memories, agents, and tools pass regression tests under multi-user isolation.
  • [ ] Requirements, API, ERD, HLD, LLD, and acceptance tests have an explicit traceability mapping.
  • [ ] Documentation distinguishes implemented behavior from target-state design.

docs.title: Appendix A — Key Design Rules
docs.text:
1. VIRA Server is the platform; clients are endpoints. Endpoint collection runs on devices; central identity, policy, persistence, and orchestration run on the server.
  2. A username is not a device identity. A device ID is not proof of device identity either; its credential proves that identity.
  3. source is not authentication. It is descriptive metadata. Device identity is derived from validated credentials.
  4. User identity is not inferred from device ownership. Background events can have no user actor; interactive actions use authenticated user context.
  5. Authorization is evaluated at every resource boundary, including streams. Authentication alone never grants access to all events.
  6. Events are first-class data. Define event IDs, schema version, source, device/user attribution, timing, retention, deduplication, and delivery semantics before building clients.
  7. One canonical design across artifacts. API, schema, HLD, LLD, tests, and docs must evolve from the same requirement IDs and contract definitions.

docs.title: VIRA Multi-Device Implementation Notes
docs.text: Implements docs/dev/designs/multi-device-design.md against the current code base. The server is a platform; endpoint devices connect through /api/v1. The server installation is itself an endpoint device (devices.is_server_local = 1): its in-process sensors publish through the same EventIngestionService as remote devices (via LocalDeviceDispatcher), so server events have device provenance, the same allow-list, deduplication and retention.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text: Area Change Files Schema Versioned migrations (schema_migrations): users.public_id/status/deleted_at, devices, device_credentials, user_device_access, device_events, device_latest_state, messages.created_by_device_id, memories.device_id, outbox_events.device_id, extra auth_audit columns, WAL mode auth/migrations.py, auth/database.py Identity Typed principals (UserPrincipal, DevicePrincipal, ServicePrincipal); bootstrap-once (atomic); disabled/deleted users cannot authenticate; password change revokes sessions auth/principals.py, auth/auth.py Admin User create/list/get/update/delete (soft), last-admin protection, audit auth/admin.py, api/routes_admin.py Devices Register (credential shown once, hash stored), list/get/rename, rotate (step-up password), revoke, retire, access grants (owner/operator/viewer), heartbeat, capability status, state machine devices/service.py, devices/store.py, api/routes_devices.py Ingestion POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/events:batch: credential-derived device id, allow-list, schema/time/size validation, idempotent by event_id, conflict audit, event row + outbox in one transaction, per-device rate limit devices/ingestion.py, devices/policy.py, devices/ratelimit.py Server as device Local device created at boot, owned by admins, heartbeat + retention task; sensors publish via local ingestion devices/local_device.py, kernel/kernel.py Isolation SSE filtered per user/device grant (viewer payloads redacted, revocation honoured); agent.response addressed to the requester only; admin-only kernel/config/ops routes; /config redacts secrets; device-scoped memories devices/visibility.py, api/streams.py, api/app.py, auth/database.py Chat Optional device_id validated against grants; stored on messages; POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/messages api/app.py Agents Router passes device_id/actor_user_id; scheduler queues events instead of dropping them; ChatAgent is re-entrant (no per-request instance state); a failed event no longer disables an agent agent_orchestration/*, agent/* API conventions /api/v1 aliases for legacy routes, error body {detail, error:{code,message,correlation_id}}, server-side X-Correlation-ID, cursor pagination api/deps.py Client Reference endpoint client: enroll, secure credential file, offline SQLite queue, backoff, heartbeat clients/endpoint_agent.py Flutter client VIRA Link: device enrollment, modular capture, offline outbox, heartbeat, batch sync, device management. Targets Android, iOS, web, Linux and Windows. client/

docs.title: Requirement traceability (implemented)
docs.text: FR-ID-01..07, FR-DEV-01..08, FR-EVT-01..08 and 10, FR-APP-01..03, NFR-SEC-01/02/04, NFR-REL-01, NFR-OBS-01, NFR-COMP-01 map to the tests in vira/tests/test_multi_device.py (46 tests).

docs.title: Not implemented / known limits
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL adapter, external broker, time-series store (SQLite/WAL only; design lists these as production options).
  • Idempotency-Key for POST /devices (chat already requires it).
  • Request-level rate limiting for user APIs and login throttling (device ingest and heartbeat are limited; limiter is in-process).
  • TLS termination, https_only cookies and CSRF protection are deployment/config work.
  • Hard user deletion / retention workflow (delete is a tombstone; conversations and memories are kept).
  • A web UI for user/device administration (use the API).
  • The unversioned legacy routes remain as adapters; the web UI still uses them.
  • docs/dev/architecture/system-design.md / docs/dev/architecture/framework.md / diagrams were not rewritten.

docs.title: Operating notes
docs.text:
• After upgrading, existing users are kept (all are admin); each gets a public_id. Run once; migrations are idempotent.
  • Create users: POST /api/v1/admin/users. Enrol a laptop: python -m vira.clients.endpoint_agent enroll --server http://HOST:8000 --username alice, or use the Flutter companion in client/ (VIRA Link) on Android, iOS, web, Linux or Windows.
  • Set auth.secret_key and serve behind TLS before exposing remote devices.
  • Run tests: python -m unittest vira.tests.test_multi_device -v.

docs.title: P4 — Ecosystem and scale
docs.text: This phase makes VIRA extensible and deployable beyond a single household.

docs.title: Plugin and extension API
docs.text:
See PLUGIN_SDK.md. Highlights:

  • manifest-based plugin discovery (vira-plugin.json)
  • stable Plugin / PluginContext SDK
  • declared permissions enforced before load
  • tools, HTTP routes, sensors, agents, prompt specialists, events and jobs
  • enable/disable/reload without restarting tools and agents
  • plugin state and data directories
  • compatibility and dependency checks
  • failure isolation per plugin

docs.title: MCP tool marketplace and allow-lists
docs.text:
The server ships a curated catalogue of reference MCP servers (filesystem, git, fetch, memory, sequential-thinking, SQLite, browser automation, time).

GET  /api/v1/mcp/marketplace?q=browser
POST /api/v1/mcp/servers                  install from marketplace or manually
GET  /api/v1/mcp/servers
POST /api/v1/mcp/servers/{id}/connect
POST /api/v1/mcp/servers/{id}/disconnect
POST /api/v1/mcp/servers/{id}/enable
POST /api/v1/mcp/servers/{id}/disable

Installed servers are disabled by default after marketplace installation so an administrator can review command, arguments and permissions before connecting.

Tool policies support default, user, role and org subjects with precedence user > org > role > default. A policy can allow/deny a whole server or specific tool names. Server-level allowed_tools and denied_tools apply before user policies. Tools without any policy remain allowed, preserving pre-P4 installations.

docs.title: Organizations and teams
docs.text:
GET/POST        /api/v1/organizations
GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/organizations/{id}
POST            /api/v1/organizations/{id}/members
PATCH/DELETE    /api/v1/organizations/{id}/members/{user_id}

Roles: owner, admin, member. Org-scoped resources use the X-Organization-ID header:

  • durable workflows (/api/v1/workflows)
  • RAG documents and search (/api/v1/rag)
  • object storage (/api/v1/objects)
  • LLM usage summaries (/api/v1/usage/summary)

Personal resources keep organization_id = NULL, so existing behavior is unchanged.

docs.title: Object storage
docs.text:
The objects API stores attachments, exports and large artifacts:

POST   /api/v1/objects              multipart file upload
GET    /api/v1/objects              list personal or org objects
GET    /api/v1/objects/{id}         download
DELETE /api/v1/objects/{id}

Backends:

  • local (default): ./data/objects, SHA-256 addresses
  • s3: AWS S3, MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze S3 and compatible services
VIRA_OBJECT_STORE=s3
VIRA_S3_BUCKET=vira
VIRA_S3_ACCESS_KEY=...
VIRA_S3_SECRET_KEY=...
VIRA_S3_REGION=us-east-1
VIRA_S3_ENDPOINT=https://s3.example.com
VIRA_S3_PREFIX=vira/
VIRA_S3_PATH_STYLE=1

The S3 backend uses SigV4 directly (no SDK dependency). Metadata lives in the database; bytes live in the backend.

docs.title: Horizontal scaling, broker and replicas
docs.text:
The API process is stateless apart from the shared database. Run one or more workers:

python -m vira.worker --interval 5

Durable jobs are claimed atomically, so multiple workers can run safely.

Broker selection:

VIRA_BROKER=database   # default, shared DB jobs table
VIRA_BROKER=redis      # requires the redis package; VIRA_REDIS_URL
VIRA_BROKER=nats       # requires the nats package; VIRA_NATS_URL

PostgreSQL read-replica routing for reporting helpers:

VIRA_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...
VIRA_DATABASE_READ_URL=postgresql://replica...

SQLite remains the default for local installs.

docs.title: Update channel
docs.text:
Administrators publish releases to channels (stable, beta, dev) for server and client:

POST   /api/v1/updates/releases
GET    /api/v1/updates/releases
DELETE /api/v1/updates/releases/{id}
GET    /api/v1/updates/check?product=client&channel=stable&current_version=1.2.0

Checks use semantic version ordering (including prereleases). min_version prevents offering an update to installations that must upgrade through an intermediate release.

docs.title: Cost and quota dashboard
docs.text:
Every LLM call records provider, model, prompt/completion tokens, estimated cost, latency, user, organization and agent in llm_usage. The same dashboard also reports object-storage bytes/count and device-event volume for the personal, organization or fleet scope.

GET /api/v1/usage/summary?days=30        personal or org dashboard
GET /api/v1/admin/usage?days=30          fleet dashboard
GET /api/v1/admin/quotas
PUT /api/v1/admin/quotas                 user/org/global, day/month

Quotas can limit tokens, cost or both. A call that would exceed a quota is rejected with HTTP 429 (quota_exceeded). Cost rates default to a built-in table and can be overridden with VIRA_LLM_RATES JSON (USD per 1M tokens).

docs.title: Sandbox execution environments
docs.text:
Status: implemented

The sandbox is VIRA's local execution environment for agents. It is built for development work: writing projects, running builds and tests, installing dependencies, starting background servers, and archiving the resulting workspace. It is not a virtual machine and must not be used for hostile code. Use a container or VM for a stronger boundary.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
AgentTool("sandbox")
        │
        ▼
SandboxManager  ── ownership, policy, file operations, jobs, archive
        │
        ▼
BubblewrapBackend ── namespace, mounts, limits, process execution
        │
        ▼
$sandbox.root/<sandbox_id>/
    metadata.json        # lifecycle, policy, owner, timestamps, counters
    workspace/           # bind-mounted at /workspace
    artifacts/           # bind-mounted at /artifacts

A sandbox is persistent across tool calls and server restarts. On start-up the backend scans metadata.json files and restores the registry. Sandboxes that were running when the server stopped are marked idle.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Each sandbox records both the owning agent and (when available) the signed-in user. Every tool call provides the caller identity; explicit IDs that belong to another agent or user are rejected. Omitting sandbox_id reuses the current sandbox for (agent_id, user_id) or creates one on demand.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Bubblewrap provides:

  • a private PID, UTS, IPC and (by default) network namespace;
  • read-only /usr, /bin, /lib, /usr/local and /etc;
  • an empty /tmp, private /home, /root, /run, /var, /opt, /srv, /mnt, /media, /data and a hidden sandbox root;
  • only the sandbox workspace and artifacts are writable bind mounts;
  • cleared environment (--clearenv) with a minimal allow-list plus explicit variables supplied by the caller;
  • --cap-drop ALL, --die-with-parent and a new session;
  • RLIMIT CPU, address space and process counts, plus a wall-clock timeout.

The workspace is always mounted before the sandbox root is hidden; Bubblewrap resolves bind sources in the new namespace.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
SandboxPolicy is immutable and stored with each sandbox. Defaults come from config.yaml and can be overridden per sandbox at creation.

Field Default Meaning network_enabled false Attach a network namespace with outbound access timeout_seconds 900 Maximum wall clock per command max_processes 128 Process/thread headroom for the sandbox cpu_seconds 600 RLIMIT_CPU per process memory_mb 2048 RLIMIT_AS address-space limit allow_package_install true Allow pip/npm installs allow_shell true Allow shell strings (bash -lc) workspace_quota_mb 2048 Soft quota for project files after writes max_output_bytes 200000 Per-stream output cap

Changing a policy requires operation="update"; it is not silently mutated by an execute call.

docs.title: Tool surface
docs.text:
The sandbox tool has one explicit operation field. Paths are always relative to the workspace (absolute /workspace/... is accepted and normalized).

Group Operations Lifecycle create, sandboxes, info, update, delete Files write, write_many, read, list, stat, search, mkdir, delete_file, move, copy Execution execute, install, jobs, job, job_logs, job_kill Persistence archive, restore, usage

Common aliases (run, exec, bash, ls, cat, mv, cp, rm, stats, export, import) are normalized rather than rejected, so small models can recover from naming mistakes.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
• A command string runs as /bin/bash -lc "<script>" inside the sandbox, so pipes, &&, redirections and multi-line build scripts work.
  • A command array is executed directly with no shell.
  • cwd must stay inside /workspace or /artifacts.
  • env is validated and merged over the minimal sandbox environment.
  • stdin is supported for interactive-looking scripts and patch application.
  • execute returns exit_code, stdout, stderr, truncated and duration_ms. A non-zero exit is reported as a tool error so the agent can correct it.
  • background=true starts a job and returns a job_id. Use job, job_logs and job_kill to poll, read and stop it. Output is capped and both streams are drained concurrently to avoid pipe deadlocks.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
install supports two ecosystems:

  • pip (default/auto): creates /workspace/.venv on first use and installs into it. Python commands are rewritten to the venv interpreter when an agent asks to install packages and run a Python script in the same call.
  • npm: installs into /workspace/node_modules with --prefix /workspace.

Install commands run with network access enabled for that operation only, even when the sandbox policy disables network. apt is intentionally unsupported because host system paths are read-only.

docs.title: Archives
docs.text: archive writes $root/<sandbox_id>.tar.gz. Dependency and cache directories (.venv, node_modules, __pycache__, etc.) are excluded by default; pass include_dependencies=true to keep them. restore validates every member, rejects path traversal, device files, FIFOs and links, and creates a new sandbox owned by the caller.

docs.title: Agent permission
docs.text:
VIRA has three layers, all of which remain in force:

  1. Tool permission — ToolPermission(actions=["read", "write", "execute"]) and the runtime's tool.use.<tool>.<agent> check.
  2. Agent tool list — ChatAgent accepts a tools config block:
  3. allow: patterns available to this agent ([] = every registered tool);
  4. deny: patterns always removed;
  5. pinned: tools always offered to the tool loop even when the dynamic catalog would not rank them.

config.yaml pins sandbox for the Chatbot, so code/build requests use a real environment instead of only discussing code. 3. Human approval — sandbox operations are destructive by classification, but the shipped configuration lists sandbox in security.approvals.safe_tools because the environment is isolated with its own filesystem, namespaces and resource limits. That lets a ChatAgent build and run projects without a prompt for every file or command. Remove it from safe_tools to restore per-call approval; destructive_tools and security.approvals.tools.sandbox can also force approval for selected operations. Shell and host-filesystem tools remain gated either way.

Long builds are bounded by tool_timeouts in the ChatAgent config (sandbox: 600 seconds by default in the shipped configuration) and by the sandbox's own timeout_seconds.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Docker deployments must mount a writable volume at sandbox.root and allow unprivileged user namespaces (see the Bubblewrap troubleshooting hint).
  • On Ubuntu 24.04+, AppArmor may require kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0 or a bwrap profile.
  • Deleted sandboxes remove their workspace and archive. Archives restored after restart are discovered from disk, not from a database.
  • The host process never accepts a host path from the model; all file operations resolve inside the workspace and reject symlink escapes.

docs.title: Wayland sensor design
docs.text: VIRA's behavioral context is built from coarse, local signals rather than capturing the user's screen. This is intentional: Wayland clients cannot enumerate or inspect other applications through the core protocol. Screen capture is mediated by xdg-desktop-portal and PipeWire, requires an explicit user selection/consent flow, and is not a suitable background sensor.

docs.title: Signals and collection modes
docs.text:
Sensor Mode Default Useful context Privacy decision FileSystemSensor event-driven opt-in files created, edited, moved, deleted in an approved workspace paths are scoped; never watch $HOME by default WaylandIdleSensor polling, change-only events 5 s present/idle transitions and session identity no global keyboard or pointer capture UserActivitySensor polling 2 s clipboard-change frequency and content length wl-paste only; content is suppressed by default ProcessSensor polling 15 s process count and coarse resource pressure only top resource consumers, no command lines NetworkSensor polling 10 s network intensity and online-work periods byte/packet counters only, no destinations HardwareSensor polling 30 s CPU, memory, battery, thermal and display conditions low-rate aggregate telemetry

Project context should come from an explicitly configured FileSystemSensor, not from a home-directory scan. Global focus and screenshot sensors are not implemented because Wayland does not provide those capabilities to ordinary background clients.

docs.title: Signals deliberately not collected
docs.text:
• Screenshots, OCR, and video capture.
  • Global keyboard and pointer events.
  • Global active-window enumeration or application titles.
  • X11 APIs (xclip, xsel, Xlib, or XTest).
  • Clipboard contents unless a future, explicit user-consent setting enables bounded content capture.

If a user needs screen context, it should be a foreground, user-initiated portal session using org.freedesktop.portal.ScreenCast, not a silent sensor. The portal's source selection and consent must remain visible to the user.

docs.title: Configuration guidance
docs.text:
The default values in config.yaml balance behavioral resolution with event volume:

  • Event-driven filesystem changes are the primary fine-grained work signal.
  • Idle and clipboard polling are fast enough to segment sessions without producing a one-event-per-second stream.
  • Process and network samples are slower because they describe trends.
  • Hardware samples are slowest because they are environmental context, not direct user intent.

Keep payloads aggregate and apply retention at the device event policy. Any new sensor should document its signal, collection mode, data minimization, and Wayland support before being enabled by default.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Wayland protocol overview
  • Wayland idle-notify protocol
  • Desktop portal ScreenCast interface
  • PipeWire

docs.title: Workspaces, sandboxes and host tools
docs.text:
The durable unit is a workspace, not an agent. A workspace is a directory on the host that users can open, back up or version. Sandboxes are execution contexts attached to a workspace.

workspace (shared directory, user-visible)
├── agent A sandbox (isolated namespace) ── same files
├── agent B sandbox (isolated namespace) ── same files
└── user opens the directory directly

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
vira/workspace/service.py:

  • plain name my-project → workspace.root/my-project
  • absolute path or ~/... → used as-is when workspace.allow_user_paths: true
  • no workspace supplied → <root>/user-<id>, shared by every agent for that user
workspace:
  root: "~/VIRA/workspaces"
  allow_user_paths: true
  default_execution_mode: bubblewrap   # bubblewrap | host

The user can select a workspace per chat turn:

{ "message": "work on this", "workspace": "/home/me/code/project" }

The API puts it in the event, and it is injected into every sandbox tool call for that run, so the model does not have to repeat it. A workspace id is also accepted.

The API exposes:

  • GET /api/v1/workspaces
  • POST /api/v1/workspaces {name, path?, execution_mode?}
  • PATCH /api/v1/workspaces/{id} {execution_mode}

docs.title: Sharing across agents
docs.text:
sandbox resolves the workspace and creates one sandbox per agent/workspace pair. Each sandbox has its own process namespace and artifacts directory, but all of them bind the same workspace directory:

  • two agents see the same files;
  • different projects use different workspace names;
  • deleting one sandbox never deletes a shared workspace.

docs.title: Host tools
docs.text: There are two ways to expose host-installed tools (Node, Python, compilers, SDKs, etc.).

docs.title: 1. Host execution mode
docs.text:
workspace:
  default_execution_mode: host

or per workspace:

curl -X PATCH /api/v1/workspaces/<id> -d '{"execution_mode":"host"}'

Commands run directly in the workspace with the host PATH. /workspace and /artifacts in commands are translated to the real directories. The sandbox still owns file operations, quotas, timeouts and job tracking. Host mode is an explicit admin / workspace choice; it is equivalent to granting shell access as the VIRA user and cannot be selected by a model (the sandbox tool strips it from policy input).

docs.title: 2. Read-only mounts in bubblewrap
docs.text:
sandbox:
  readonly_mounts: ["/opt/toolchain", "/snap"]
  extra_path: "/opt/toolchain/bin:/snap/bin"
workspace:
  default_execution_mode: bubblewrap

This keeps namespace isolation while making a host toolchain visible.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• workspace.allow_user_paths: false restricts users to names under workspace.root.
  • System directories (/etc, /usr, /, …) are rejected as workspace paths.
  • Workspaces are indexed in the workspaces table (migration 16); the filesystem is always the source of truth. Tools remain usable if the table is absent.
  • Host mode does not enforce network isolation.

docs.title: Research basis
docs.text:
The suite design follows published agent and memory evaluations:

  • ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) — interleaved reasoning and tool actions.
  • Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) — tool selection and argument quality.
  • ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) — API selection and argument correctness.
  • AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023) — task completion across environments.
  • τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024) — pass^k reliability and tool-agent-user interaction.
  • LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024/2025) — temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention.
  • RAGAS (Es et al., 2023) — context precision and faithfulness for RAG answers.

See docs/dev/evaluations/research-basis.md for the mapping.

docs.title: Evaluation research basis
docs.text: Phase 5's evaluation harness applies published agent-evaluation ideas to a local-first, tool-using assistant. The goal is not to reproduce a benchmark leaderboard; it is to make tool selection, task completion, memory retrieval, failure recovery and safety measurable on every commit without a model or network.

docs.title: Papers and what VIRA adopts
docs.text: Paper Idea adopted VIRA implementation ReAct — Yao et al., 2022 (arXiv:2210.03629) Interleave reasoning with actions; observations drive the next step. The agent loop already emits thought + one tool call + observation per step. Evaluation checks multi-step completion and failure recovery. Toolformer — Schick et al., 2023 (arXiv:2302.04761) The model decides whether and which tool to call. tool_selection measures top-1 and top-3 routing over a representative catalogue. ToolBench / ToolLLM — Qin et al., 2023 (arXiv:2307.16789) API selection and argument correctness in a large tool space. tool_selection checks routing; generated tools validate parameters and only support one safe HTTPS GET shape. AgentBench — Liu et al., 2023 (arXiv:2308.03688) Multi-environment task completion rather than single-turn QA. task_completion runs device, database, RAG and web agent-loop tasks end to end. τ-bench — Yao et al., 2024 (arXiv:2406.12045) Tool-agent-user interaction and pass^k reliability. The harness runs every suite twice and reports repeat_stable; the live benchmark supports --runs 10. LongMemEval — Wu et al., 2024/2025 (arXiv:2410.10813) Long-term memory includes information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention. memory_retrieval covers single-session, multi-session, knowledge update, recency, abstention and user feedback. RAGAS — Es et al., 2023 (arXiv:2309.15217) RAG quality needs context relevance, faithfulness and answer relevance. task_completion checks that RAG questions call rag_search and answer from the retrieved note; the RAG service enforces per-user scoping. Reflexion — Shinn et al., 2023 (arXiv:2303.11366) Learn from failed attempts rather than repeating them. The loop blocks repeated calls and stores lessons; failure_recovery covers error correction, repeated calls, malformed JSON and invented tools. SWE-bench — Jimenez et al., 2023 (arXiv:2310.06770) Task completion is only credible when an executable check passes. Every case is deterministic and executable; CI runs the full evaluation in vira/tests/test_phase5.py. WebArena — Zhou et al., 2023 (arXiv:2307.13854) Realistic tool environments expose failure modes that toy prompts miss. Web cases are deterministic scripts that simulate search failure and recovery, rather than depending on network availability.

docs.title: What this harness does not claim
docs.text:
• It is not a model-quality leaderboard. The deterministic suites use scripted replies so they can run in CI. Real model quality is measured by scripts/benchmark.py --runs N.
  • It does not prove prompt-injection resistance. It verifies approval gates, safe tool schemas and scoped retrieval; adversarial model behaviour remains a research problem.
  • It does not reproduce LongMemEval's full dataset. It adopts its five memory abilities as test categories and uses small, inspectable fixtures.
  • It does not replace penetration testing or a formal security review.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
python3 scripts/evaluate.py
python3 scripts/evaluate.py --json
python3 scripts/evaluate.py --write
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_phase5 -v

Results are recorded in:

  • docs/dev/evaluations/agent-platform.md
  • docs/dev/evaluations/agent-platform.json

The JSON report includes the git revision, VIRA version, Python/platform, per-case results and whether the deterministic suites were stable across a repeat run, so two releases can be compared directly.

docs.title: Agent roadmap — daily-use agents
docs.text:
Status: active implementation plan Last updated: 2026-11-21 Scope: proactive, recurring agents that make VIRA useful every day.

Current status: P0–P5 are implemented and tested. The five daily-use agents are available.

This roadmap turns the paper-aligned agent architectures and VIRA's device, memory, knowledge and tool platform into five daily-use agents. It deliberately puts shared prerequisites first: without scheduling, delivery, safety and discovery, every agent would become a one-off demo.

Related documents:

  • Agent architectures
  • Agent design
  • Product roadmap
  • Server roadmap

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Proactive but opt-in. A recurring agent only runs after the user creates or enables a schedule.
  2. Local-first and permissioned. Agents use the same user/device scopes, consent, approvals and audit as chat.
  3. Bounded. Every run has worker, round, time and token limits.
  4. Observable. Every scheduled run has a durable run record, timeline and notification.
  5. Architecture-aware. The agent's coordination topology is explicit (single, centralized, etc.) and recorded with the run.
  6. One useful output per trigger. A daily agent should produce a short result the user can act on, not a wall of text.

docs.title: P0 — Prerequisites (must ship first)
docs.text: These are shared by all five agents. None of them is agent-specific.

docs.title: P0.1 Durable agent schedule store
docs.text:
• [x] agent_schedules table: owner, agent, schedule spec, timezone, quiet hours, channels, task profile, enabled state, next run and lock.
  • [x] agent_schedule_runs table: per-run status, result/error, run id, notification id and timestamps.
  • [x] SQLite migration and PostgreSQL schema parity.
  • [x] Strict user/organization scoping on every read and write.

Acceptance: a schedule survives restart; another user cannot read, change, run or delete it.

docs.title: P0.2 Proactive scheduler loop
docs.text:
• [x] In-process scheduler owned by the agent orchestrator (not a second runtime).
  • [x] Atomic claim of due schedules with lock expiry, so a crash retries instead of losing the run or double-running forever.
  • [x] Bounded concurrency, timeouts and failures recorded per run.
  • [x] Daily, weekly and interval schedules with IANA timezones and quiet hours.
  • [x] next_run_at advanced using the schedule's timezone, not server-local time.

Acceptance: a daily 08:00 schedule runs once per day in its timezone; a server restart does not silently lose a due schedule.

docs.title: P0.3 Proactive task contract
docs.text:
• [x] RuntimeScheduler.run_task() executes a TaskRequest with the same identity, lifecycle and error handling as chat.
  • [x] Scheduled requests carry user_id, organization_id, run_id, trigger metadata and an optional task profile.
  • [x] The agent's architecture and coordination data are recorded in the run.
  • [x] Proactive runs appear in the durable run timeline.

Acceptance: any registered BaseAgent can be scheduled without a new adapter or a special "cron agent" implementation.

docs.title: P0.4 Notification delivery
docs.text:
• [x] In-app notifications are delivered immediately and remain unread until opened.
  • [x] External delivery uses a provider interface; webhook is the first provider.
  • [x] Retries, attempts and last error are stored; duplicates are suppressed with a dedupe key.
  • [x] Worker periodically delivers pending notifications.
  • [x] Quiet hours suppress or defer scheduled notifications.

Acceptance: a scheduled run creates an in-app notification; a configured webhook receives the same payload; a failed webhook is retried and then marked failed.

docs.title: P0.5 Discovery and onboarding metadata
docs.text:
• [x] A machine-readable catalog of the five recommended agents: pitch, daily trigger, required tools, default schedule, architecture and status.
  • [x] API endpoint for the catalog and for schedule CRUD/run-now.
  • [x] Documentation that explains the first useful setup in under five minutes.

Acceptance: a client can list the recommended agents, create a schedule for an installed agent, and show the next run time without reading source code.

docs.title: P0.6 Safety and control
docs.text:
• [x] Schedules are user-scoped and require an authenticated user.
  • [x] Mutation endpoints are rate-limited by the existing middleware.
  • [x] Proactive runs use the same tool permissions, approvals and audit as chat.
  • [x] Users can disable or delete a schedule at any time.
  • [x] Notification content is not exposed across users.

Acceptance: disabling a schedule stops future runs; destructive tools still require approval during a proactive run.

docs.title: P0 implementation notes
docs.text:
• Schedule store and math: vira/agent/schedules.py.
  • In-process scheduler: vira/agent/proactive.py, owned by AgentOrchestratorModule.
  • Typed proactive runs: RuntimeScheduler.run_task().
  • Delivery: vira/notifications.py plus the notifications.deliver worker job.
  • API: vira/api/routes_schedules.py (/api/v1/agent-schedules, /api/v1/agent-recipes).
  • Schema: migrations 17–18 and PostgreSQL parity.
  • Tests: vira/tests/test_agent_schedules.py.

docs.title: P1 — Morning Brief — implemented
docs.text:
Pitch: "Open VIRA with your coffee. It already knows what matters today."

Daily trigger: daily at a user-selected time (default 07:30).

Output: a short brief covering calendar, tasks, device/fleet health, yesterday's focus context and the first three actions.

Architecture: SingleAgent with tools by default. Switch to CentralizedAgentSystem only when the user connects many sources and the profile justifies the coordination cost.

Uses: insights, user_context, device events, memory, knowledge, optional MCP calendar/task/email connectors.

Implementation: - Agent: vira/agent/Agents/morning_brief.py, registered as morning-brief in config.yaml. - Collects configured context_tools, labels missing/erroring sources as UNAVAILABLE, and synthesizes with the LLM. - Deterministic fallback brief when the model is unavailable. - Returns source names and unavailable reasons in TaskResult.data. - End-to-end schedule delivery is covered by vira/tests/test_morning_brief.py.

  • [x] One notification per day, deduplicated across restarts.
  • [x] Every claim is traceable to a tool result or labelled as unavailable.
  • [x] The user can mute, pause or change the time from the API/client.
  • [x] Deterministic fallback keeps the habit working without a model.
  • [x] Optional calendar/task/email MCP tools via context_tools.

Acceptance evidence: python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_morning_brief -v.

Metrics: daily active briefs, open rate, 7/30-day retention.

docs.title: P2 — Focus and Wellbeing Coach — implemented
docs.text:
Pitch: "Your agent sees your actual screen time, focus and device signals — privately."

Daily triggers: morning focus plan, optional mid-day check-in and evening review. Weekly report on demand or scheduled.

Architecture: SingleAgent for coaching. Weekly report may use CentralizedAgentSystem when there are multiple devices or categories.

Uses: VIRA Link app usage, screen sessions, focus sessions, battery/idle signals, insights, memory of goals.

Implementation: - Agent: vira/agent/Agents/focus_coach.py, registered as focus-coach. - Schedule input.mode selects morning, checkin, evening or weekly. - Context comes from user_context + insights; goals come from memory. - Weekly mode requests insights with include_apps=false, so app names are hidden; categories and measured numbers remain. - Quiet hours are enforced by the proactive scheduler before the run starts. - Deterministic fallback when the model is unavailable.

  • [x] Recommendations reference measured data, not generic advice.
  • [x] Break reminders respect quiet hours and notification settings.
  • [x] Weekly report can be exported without raw app titles.
  • [x] Morning/checkin/evening/weekly modes share one agent and one schedule API.

Acceptance evidence: python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_focus_second_brain -v.

Metrics: daily active coaching users, focus sessions started, weekly report views.

docs.title: P3 — Second Brain and Memory Curator — implemented
docs.text:
Pitch: "Tell VIRA once. It remembers — locally, with your permission."

Daily triggers: capture is user-initiated; a weekly consolidation runs on a schedule.

Architecture: SingleAgent for capture and retrieval; consolidation stays single-agent because it is sequential.

Uses: scoped knowledge base, memory ranking/feedback, RAG, conversation history, export/delete.

Implementation: - Agent: vira/agent/Agents/second_brain.py, registered as second-brain. - input.mode selects capture, ask, correct or consolidate. - Capture writes verified personal knowledge with requested_by_user=true. - Recall uses merged knowledge search and answers with numbered citations and stored dates; no hits means no model call and an honest "not found". - Correction creates a superseding revision; the old item is retained and deprecated. Added PATCH /api/v1/knowledge/items/{item_id}. - Consolidation lists personal knowledge through the authorized service API and reports duplicates, stale items and low-confidence items. It deletes nothing. - Added knowledge_list to the runtime/service so read access follows the same authorization path as search and write.

  • [x] "What did I decide about X?" returns the source item and date.
  • [x] Users can inspect, correct and delete what VIRA remembers.
  • [x] Weekly consolidation reports duplicates and stale items without deleting anything automatically.
  • [x] Capture and recall are scoped to the authenticated user.

Acceptance evidence: python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_focus_second_brain vira.tests.test_knowledge -v.

Metrics: captures per active user, retrieval success, 30-day retention, memory items per user.

docs.title: P4 — Chief of Staff (inbox, calendar, tasks) — implemented
docs.text:
Pitch: "Your agent triages the day and drafts the boring replies — you approve what sends."

Daily triggers: morning triage and evening follow-up.

Architecture: CentralizedAgentSystem for parallel thread/category triage with an orchestrator validation pass; SingleAgent for quick replies.

Uses: MCP email/calendar/task connectors, memory of people and preferences, approval gates, audit.

Implementation: - Agent: vira/agent/Agents/chief_of_staff.py, registered as chief-of-staff. - Collects configured connectors, runs one extraction worker per source in parallel, validates source attribution, then renders a triage brief. - Extracts action items with source labels/links and draft replies. - Never calls a send tool: sent=0 is recorded and drafts are output only. - Recalls preference memories for tone. - Missing connectors are reported as unavailable instead of failing the run. - Reference connector: examples/mcp/office_server.py reads local JSON emails.json, calendar.json and tasks.json without network access.

  • [x] Drafts never send without explicit approval.
  • [x] Action items are extracted with source attribution/links.
  • [x] Connector failures degrade gracefully and are reported in the brief.
  • [x] Parallel extraction with a centralized validation bottleneck.

Acceptance evidence: python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_chief_household vira.tests.test_examples -v.

Metrics: drafts accepted, time saved, connector adoption, daily active users.

docs.title: P5 — Household and Life Admin — implemented
docs.text:
Pitch: "The family operations agent that lives on your own server."

Daily triggers: morning plan and evening check; weekly household review.

Architecture: SingleAgent for everyday questions; CentralizedAgentSystem for the weekly plan (meals, budget and chores in parallel).

Uses: family/household data, memory, local files, MCP tools, reminders.

Implementation: - Agent: vira/agent/Agents/household.py, registered as household. - Reads a membership-checked household snapshot: notes, reminders and open checklist items. - input.mode selects morning, evening or weekly; input.household_id selects a household. - Weekly mode fans out to meals, budget and chores workers, then merges them and records a centralized coordination profile. - Deterministic fallback when the model is unavailable. - Delivered per member through their own schedule and quiet hours.

  • [x] Multiple household members share notes, lists and reminders.
  • [x] Non-members cannot read household data.
  • [x] Weekly review is delivered to each member according to their own quiet hours (each member owns a schedule).
  • [x] Shared data is read through the family store membership checks.

Acceptance evidence: python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_chief_household -v.

Metrics: households with 2+ active members, weekly review open rate, retention.

docs.title: Delivery order
docs.text:
1. P0 prerequisites.
  2. P1 Morning Brief — fastest daily habit and the best demo.
  3. P2 Focus Coach — strongest VIRA Link differentiator.
  4. P3 Second Brain — compounding retention.
  5. P4 Chief of Staff — largest time saving, integration-heavy.
  6. P5 Household — multi-user growth.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Unbounded autonomous loops.
  • Multi-agent coordination by default.
  • Sending messages, spending money or changing settings without approval.
  • Always-on sensing or notification permission without an explicit user action.
  • A hosted multi-tenant SaaS control plane.

docs.title: VIRA Link Roadmap
docs.text:
Goal: make VIRA Link a mature, privacy-first device companion that collects useful behavioural and device context locally, works offline, and gives the VIRA server enough structured data to power useful agents later.

Legend: Done · Now · Next · Later

docs.title: 1. Product principles
docs.text:
1. Local first. Capture writes to the device outbox before any network call.
  2. Explicit consent. Every sensitive signal has its own switch and OS permission. App usage is opt-in at the OS level through Usage Access.
  3. Minimum necessary data. Prefer aggregates and metadata over raw content. Never collect keystrokes, message bodies, passwords or clipboard content by default.
  4. Server is authoritative. Device identity, credentials, scopes and event policy come from the VIRA server.
  5. Modular collectors. A feature should be addable or removable without touching sync, storage or the UI shell.
  6. Explainable insights. Every summary must be traceable to events the user can inspect, export or delete.
  7. Graceful degradation. Unsupported platforms report unavailable, not fake data.

docs.title: 2.1 Device and runtime context
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Platform, OS, device type, hostname Correct interpretation of all other data Low Done App/client version, protocol Compatibility and rollout health Low Done Hardware: CPU, memory, uptime Device health, performance warnings Low Done (Linux/Windows; macOS storage) Battery level, charging, power source Energy advice, quiet-hours logic Low Done (Android/Linux) Network type, interface availability Offline/online context, sync scheduling Low Done (basic) Screen on/off, unlock count Screen time, rest reminders Medium Done (Android) Idle/focus state Focus sessions, interruption detection Medium Done (desktop idle + focus sessions) Crash/error events Reliability and support Low Done (opt-in, redacted, local or explicit upload)

docs.title: 2.2 Application and activity context
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Foreground app time per package “Most used apps”, digital wellbeing, study advice High Done (Android) App category (social, education, games…) Human-readable summaries and recommendations Medium Done Current foreground app Real-time focus/context signals High Next App launches and sessions Habit and routine detection High Next Desktop active window/app Equivalent of Android app usage on desktop High Done (X11, Sway, Hyprland, KDE, Windows, macOS; GNOME Wayland via bundled extension) Media playback Entertainment vs work balance Medium Later Browser/domain usage Online learning vs distraction High, opt-in Later

docs.title: 2.3 Communication and social context
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Notification volume and source app Interruption/attention analysis High, opt-in Later Call/meeting duration Workload and meeting load High, opt-in Later Message counts by app, never content Communication balance High, opt-in Later Contact interaction frequency, never content Relationship maintenance Very high, opt-in Later

docs.title: 2.4 Productivity, learning and planning
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Study/focus sessions Student coaching, streaks Medium Next Tasks completed / reminders Planning and follow-through Medium Later Calendar busy/free blocks Meeting load, focus suggestions High, opt-in Later Documents recently opened Knowledge recall and context High, opt-in Later Typing/activity counts, never content Focus and workload estimate Medium Later

docs.title: 2.5 Health, location and environment
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Steps, sleep, workouts Holistic wellbeing recommendations Very high, opt-in Later Location / places Routines, commute, context-aware reminders Very high, opt-in Later Ambient noise / light Focus and sleep suggestions High, opt-in Later Screen brightness and night usage Eye comfort and sleep hygiene Medium Later

docs.title: 2.6 Data quality and privacy metadata
docs.text: Signal Why it is useful Sensitivity Status Consent state per collector Trust, audit, server policy Low Done Capability status on heartbeat Know what the device can report Low Done Event retention class Privacy-aware server modelling Low Done Local export / delete User control Low Next

docs.title: 3. Use cases this unlocks
docs.text:
1. Digital wellbeing coach — daily screen time, top apps, late-night usage, category balance and weekly trends.
  2. Student focus coach — compare study/education time with social and games, suggest focus blocks and exam-week limits.
  3. Context-aware assistant — “you usually study at 7 pm; should I enable focus mode?” or “you have been on social apps for 45 minutes”.
  4. Daily and weekly reviews — the agent summarises what happened, what changed and what to try next.
  5. Habit and pattern detection — streaks, first-app-of-the-day, doom-scroll sessions, late-night screen time, weekend vs weekday patterns.
  6. Personal recommendations — learning app suggestions, break reminders, app limits, sleep hygiene, fitness routines.
  7. Task automation triggers — start a focus session when a study app opens, pause notifications during deep work, queue a review after a long session.
  8. Device fleet health — low battery, high CPU, storage pressure, stale devices, unusual activity.
  9. Security and anomaly detection — unexpected app usage bursts, revoked credential detection, unusual sync patterns.
  10. Privacy-preserving local insights — summaries on-device before sending raw events, with redaction and aggregation.

docs.title: 4. Current architecture
docs.text:
collectors -> CaptureService -> OutboxStore -> SyncService -> VIRA API
                    |                              |
                    +-> UsageLedger (local)        +-> heartbeat
                    +-> Settings (consent)
  • Collector contract: id, title, description, capability, event type, interval, default-enabled, optional access request.
  • CollectorResult reports available, unavailable, permission_denied or degraded plus a human-readable message.
  • CaptureService schedules collectors and writes events to the outbox.
  • UsageLedger keeps a 30-day local daily rollup for offline Insights.
  • SyncService batches events, retries with backoff and heartbeats capability status.
  • Insights is a module in the shell, not hard-coded navigation.

docs.title: Event naming
docs.text:
device.telemetry.state          device/app identity and status
sensor.hardware.state           CPU, memory, uptime
sensor.network.state            interface availability
device.app.usage                aggregated foreground app time
device.session.state            screen time, unlocks, current session
device.focus.state              focus/distraction summary per interval
device.battery.state             battery level, charging, temperature

docs.title: App usage event shape
docs.text:
{
  "event_id": "uuid",
  "type": "device.app.usage",
  "schema_version": 1,

  • Never collect message bodies, passwords, keystrokes or clipboard content by default.
  • Prefer device.* for durable aggregates and sensor.*/telemetry for high-volume raw signals.
  • Include retention class and capability status in the event/heartbeat contract.

docs.title: 10. How to add a collector
docs.text:
1. Create lib/services/capture/collectors/<name>_collector.dart.
  2. Implement Collector with a unique id, capability, event type and interval.
  3. Return CollectorResult.available/... and set canRequestAccess if an OS permission is needed.
  4. Add it to CaptureService._collectors.
  5. Add category/summary logic to the relevant ledger or page if needed.
  6. Write a unit test with a fake platform probe/source.
  7. Document the new event in this roadmap and in client/README.md.

Removing a collector is the reverse: remove it from CaptureService, delete the file, and remove its capability from the UI.

docs.title: VIRA Server Roadmap
docs.text:
Status: design + implementation plan for the server side of VIRA.

The client is now a mature collector and the server accepts device events, aggregates insights and exposes an admin control panel. The next work is to turn the server from a strong single-process local runtime into a durable, secure and agent-ready platform.

docs.title: 1. Current server baseline
docs.text:
Already implemented:

  • Kernel with event bus, dispatcher, scheduler, state manager, metrics, security
  • FastAPI API, authenticated dashboard/chat, sessions, users and roles
  • Multi-device platform: enrollment, credentials, heartbeat, event ingestion, idempotency, rate limits, fleet inventory and audit
  • Device event storage with policy classes, retention and outbox
  • ChatAgent tool loop, agents, registry, router, scheduler, lessons and sub-agents
  • Local/MCP tools with permissions and audit
  • Memory store, conversations, runs and incognito conversations
  • Device insight aggregation API and ChatAgent insights tool
  • Admin APIs for users, devices, audit, health, agents, tools and metrics
  • SQLite persistence with versioned migrations

The main gaps are durability, scale, consent enforcement, background work, agent quality, and operational hardening.

docs.title: 2. Guiding principles
docs.text:
1. Server is the policy authority. Clients propose / capture; the server enforces consent, access, retention and purpose.
  2. Event-first. Facts are immutable events; derived views are rebuildable.
  3. Durable by default. Acknowledged work survives process restart.
  4. Least privilege. Users, devices, agents, tools and admin actions each have explicit scopes.
  5. Observable. Every important action has a metric, log and audit trail.
  6. Local-first compatible. Postgres/Redis are optional production upgrades, not a requirement for a single-machine install.
  7. Agent safety. Agents get bounded tools, budgets, approvals and audit.

docs.title: P0 — Production foundation (must do first)
docs.text:
• [x] PostgreSQL adapter with schema (vira/db/postgres_schema.sql) and query translation while keeping SQLite for local installs. Live PostgreSQL validation remains a deployment check.
  • [x] Separate worker process for retention, rollups, backups and cleanup (python -m vira.worker). Outbox publication stays in the API process until an external broker is added.
  • [x] Durable database-backed job queue with retries, dead-letter, dedupe and periodic jobs. External Redis/Celery can replace it later.
  • [~] Schema migration runner now covers jobs, rollups and the existing versioned tables; legacy baseline DDL still lives in init_db.
  • [x] Secrets management: never store provider keys in plain config; support env/file/OS keyring and redaction in every API response.
  • [x] Encryption at rest for device credentials, provider keys, tokens and sensitive payloads; key rotation plan.
  • [x] Rate limiting for login, chat, admin, tools and insights, not only device ingestion/heartbeat.
  • [x] Structured logs, request timing metrics, request IDs and /ops/alerts; Prometheus-compatible endpoint remains the metrics API.
  • [x] Backup/restore scripts and retention jobs for SQLite.
  • [x] OpenAPI contract generated from FastAPI with a compatibility test for the critical /api/v1 paths.

Exit criteria: restart-safe jobs, Postgres option, no secrets in responses, load test with concurrent device ingestion + chat + admin.

docs.title: P1 — Device platform and consent
docs.text:
• [x] Consent registry per user/device/collector with purpose, retention, revoked_at and ingestion enforcement (consent_denied).
  • [x] Purpose and retention fields on consent rows; retention overrides event TTL at ingestion. Event-class purpose policy can be refined per type.
  • [x] Event schema registry with seeded schemas, validation on ingestion and /api/v1/event-schemas discovery.
  • [x] Server-to-device command channel: create/list commands, device claim, result reporting, expiry and cleanup (capture pause/resume, config, queue, update, export, consent).
  • [x] Pairing backend: short-lived single-use pairing codes, redeem to create a device credential, device rename/revoke/re-enrollment APIs.
  • [x] Per-user data export and deletion across devices, events, insights, conversations, memories, notifications, consents and commands.
  • [x] Retention jobs for events, sessions, jobs, commands and pairing codes; consent retention overrides event TTL.
  • [x] Insight rollups: insight_daily table and /api/v1/insights/daily.
  • [x] Fleet operations: /api/v1/admin/fleet/ops for stale devices, expiring credentials, command status and consent gaps.
  • [~] Push notification queue and device token registration are implemented; actual FCM/APNs provider delivery remains deployment work.

Exit criteria: a user can revoke a collector and the server stops accepting that data; daily summaries load from rollups; export/delete covers all stores.

docs.title: P2 — Agent platform
docs.text:
• [x] Durable agent runs: run timeline events are persisted and exposed at /api/v1/runs/{id}/events; workflow replay/resume is also available.
  • [x] Durable workflows / task graph: persisted steps, retries, compensation, replay and resume; completed steps are never re-run. API at /api/v1/workflows.
  • [x] Agent catalog and versioning: versioned markdown definitions exposed at /api/v1/agent-definitions; registry metadata is versioned.
  • [x] Specialist agents: insight coach, study coach and device doctor definitions over the insights tool; security/anomaly remains next.
  • [x] Context assembly tool: user_context returns devices, consent, battery/health and a compact usage summary.
  • [x] Persistent vector store and RAG backend: rag_documents, rag_chunks, memory_embeddings, cosine search, optional Ollama embeddings and a rag_search tool.
  • [~] Model router: provider failover and local-first routing exist; token budgets/cost accounting remain.
  • [~] Versioned agent prompts: definitions carry versions; a general prompt registry/rollback is next.
  • [ ] Guardrails: prompt injection handling, tool allow-lists, secret redaction, output validation, destructive-action approval.
  • [x] Evaluation tests for tool selection, dynamic expansion, memory ranking, specialist definitions and run events; golden conversations remain next.
  • [ ] Agent scheduler: daily/weekly reviews, reminders, anomaly checks, budgeted background reasoning.

Exit criteria: an agent run survives restart; every tool call is attributable and auditable; specialist agents answer common insight questions reliably.

  • [ ] Explainability: every recommendation links to aggregate metrics and the events/rollups that produced it.
  • [ ] Feedback loop: useful/not useful, mute a recommendation, tune thresholds; store per user and per insight type.
  • [ ] Goal and preference model: study goals, screen-time limits, focus windows, quiet hours, notification preferences.
  • [ ] Action layer: start focus session, suggest app limits, schedule break, create reminder, ask user for approval.

  • [x] MCP tool marketplace and remote tool allow-list policies: curated catalogue, install/enable/connect lifecycle and default/user/role/org policies enforced by the tool executor.
  • [x] Multi-tenant organizations/teams: organizations, membership roles and optional X-Organization-ID scoping for workflows, RAG, objects and usage.
  • [x] Object storage: local SHA-256 store plus S3-compatible SigV4 backend; /api/v1/objects upload/list/download/delete.
  • [x] Horizontal API/worker scaling: stateless API, durable multi-worker job queue, optional Redis/NATS broker adapter and PostgreSQL read-replica helper.
  • [x] Update channel for server and client versions with semver checks, channels and minimum-version gates.
  • [x] Cost/quota dashboard for LLM calls, storage and device events: usage ledger, daily/model/agent summaries, resource usage and user/org/global token and cost quotas.

Full design notes: P4_ECOSYSTEM.md.

  • [ ] Dependency/security scanning and signed release artifacts.
  • [ ] Alerting for failed outbox, credential expiry, queue backlog, agent failures and disk/database pressure.
  • [ ] Disaster recovery drill and documented RPO/RTO.
  • [ ] Tenant/user isolation tests and fuzzing for ingestion, auth and tools.
  • [ ] Accessibility and localization of server-rendered UI.

  • POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/commands — queued device command

docs.title: 6. Security and privacy checklist
docs.text:
• Consent is checked before storage, not only in the client UI.
  • Device credentials are hashed, expiring, revocable, rotated and scoped.
  • Raw event payloads are never exposed to admins by default.
  • Insight endpoints return aggregates only unless include_payload is explicitly authorized and audited.
  • Agent context is filtered by the same consent and access rules as the user.
  • Every admin, agent, tool and device action is audited with correlation IDs.
  • Sensitive data has a retention TTL and a deletion path.
  • Secrets never appear in /config, logs, tool results or chat responses.
  • Backups are encrypted and access-controlled.

docs.title: 8. Definition of done for the server
docs.text:
• Acknowledged events survive restart and are never lost silently.
  • A revoked consent stops ingestion and deletes/ages out derived data.
  • An admin can see health, jobs, agents, users, devices and audit in the UI/API.
  • A user can export and delete all their data.
  • An agent run is resumable, budgeted, explainable and auditable.
  • Insights load from rollups, not raw event scans.
  • The system passes a concurrent load test on Postgres with workers.
  • Secrets, TLS, backups and alerting are documented and tested.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• Status: PASS
  • Source: data/vira.sqlite3
  • Backup: data/backups/vira-20261120-190132.sqlite3
  • Integrity check: ok
  • Tables/rows restored: 53 / 7968
  • Missing tables: none
  • Row-count mismatches: none

docs.title: Recovery objectives
docs.text:
• RPO target: 24 hours. The worker schedules a database backup every 24 hours (jobs.backup_keep controls retention).
  • Previous backup age at drill time: none yet; this drill establishes the first restore point.
  • Measured RTO for this drill: 0.014 seconds (copy + open + integrity check, excluding container startup and DNS).

docs.title: What this proves
docs.text:
The backup is a consistent database image and it can be copied and opened independently of the live server. Row counts are compared with the live database; a serving instance may have accepted writes since the backup, so treat mismatches as informational and run the drill on an idle instance for a strict count comparison.

It does not prove that the master key is backed up. Without data/.vira_master_key (or VIRA_MASTER_KEY), encrypted fields cannot be recovered. Back up the key separately.

docs.title: VIRA threat model
docs.text:
This is a working threat model for the self-hosted VIRA Server and the VIRA Link device companion. It names assets, trust boundaries, realistic threats and the controls that exist today. It is deliberately concrete: every control points at code, a test or an operational command.

See the security overview for the user-facing version.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope

  • VIRA Server API, dashboard, chat, memory, RAG, workflows, tools, MCP, plugins.
  • Multi-user and multi-device authorization and consent.
  • Docker deployment, backups, master key and audit trail.
  • VIRA Link device enrollment, credentials and event ingestion.

Out of scope

  • A compromised host, hypervisor, Docker daemon or supply-chain compromise of the base image.
  • Physical access to an unlocked device.
  • The security of third-party cloud model providers.
  • Formal multi-tenant SaaS isolation. VIRA is local-first, not a hosted service.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text: Asset Why it matters User sessions and passwords Account takeover Device credentials Spoofed telemetry, data injection Device telemetry and insights Private behavioural data Conversations, memories and RAG documents Private personal/work content Master key (data/.vira_master_key) Decrypts sensitive fields Provider API keys and MCP secrets Financial loss, third-party access Tool execution capability Shell, filesystem, sandbox and network actions Audit and tool-call records Accountability and incident response Backups Recovery after data loss or ransomware

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
Browser / VIRA Link
        │  authenticated HTTP(S)
        ▼
VIRA Server process ── tool executor ── local tools / sandbox / MCP servers
        │                    │
        │                    └── destructive calls ── approval queue ── human
        ▼
SQLite/PostgreSQL + data volume + master key
        │
        └── optional cloud model provider (outbound)
  1. User/device ↔ server. Untrusted input: messages, events, uploaded files.
  2. Server ↔ model. Model output is untrusted. It may propose tool calls.
  3. Server ↔ tools/MCP/plugins. Tool output is untrusted and may contain prompt injection; MCP servers and plugins are separate code.
  4. Server ↔ host. Shell, filesystem and sandbox tools cross this boundary.
  5. Server ↔ backup media. Backups contain the whole database and need the master key to be useful.

docs.title: 1. Malicious prompts and tool injection
docs.text:
Threat. A user message, web page, document, memory or MCP result tells the model to ignore its instructions, call a destructive tool, exfiltrate data or hide the action from the user.

Controls

  • Tool output and retrieved text are observations, not instructions; the loop prompt says never invent tool results and never repeat identical calls.
  • Tools are allow-listed per caller and per MCP policy before execution.
  • Database tools are read-only, single-statement, admin-only for custom SQL and reject secret columns/functions.
  • Destructive local calls now stop at a human approval gate (see threat 4).
  • Every tool call is recorded with status, permission decision and caller.
  • Web tools apply SSRF checks and bounded output.

Residual risk. Prompt injection is not solved. A model can still be tricked into proposing an allowed but harmful call. Approval gates and least privilege limit the blast radius; they do not make the model trustworthy.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_security_phase3 vira.tests.test_database_query -v

docs.title: 2. Cross-user data access
docs.text:
Threat. User B reads, mutates or deletes user A's conversations, memories, RAG documents, devices, insights or workflows; or an agent's context crosses users.

Controls

  • Every chat/memory/RAG/workflow query is scoped by user_id.
  • Device access is deny-by-default through user_device_access; unknown and unauthorised devices both return 404 to avoid existence disclosure.
  • Insight routes call DeviceService.authorize before loading events.
  • Agent tool context injects the authenticated caller identity; database MCP tools never trust an identity supplied by the model.
  • SSE fan-out filters every event through visibility.authorize_event.
