Residual risk. Admin roles intentionally see fleet-wide metadata. System memories (user_id IS NULL) are visible to all active users by design.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_security_phase3 vira.tests.test_multi_device -v

docs.title: 3. Device credential leakage
docs.text:
Threat. A stolen device token injects events as another device, reads queued commands or keeps reporting after revocation.

Controls

  • Device credentials are random, scoped, expiring, revocable and stored hashed.
  • Raw tokens are shown once at enrollment.
  • Ingestion checks the path device against the credential's device.
  • Heartbeat/ingestion have separate per-device rate limits.
  • Revocation is terminal for that credential; re-enrollment issues a new one.
  • Credential rotation and expiry are visible in fleet operations.

Residual risk. A token captured before rotation is valid until it expires or is revoked. Use TLS and device disk protection.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_multi_device -v
python3 -m vira doctor

docs.title: 4. Destructive tool calls
docs.text:
Threat. The model calls shell, filesystem writes, sandbox execute/install or a custom MCP tool and changes the host, deletes data or runs untrusted code.

Controls

  • Shell is a read-only command allow-list with no shell expansion, chaining, pipes or redirects.
  • Filesystem is confined to the configured workspace root.
  • Sandbox applies CPU, memory, process and timeout limits; it is not a VM.
  • Approval gates: destructive calls create a single-use, expiring request and return APPROVAL_REQUIRED instead of executing. A user/admin must approve the exact tool + arguments in /api/v1/approvals; the next identical call consumes it once.
  • Approval arguments are redacted before storage and decisions are audited.

Residual risk. An approval is a human decision; a distracted approver can authorize a harmful call. The request shows the tool and arguments, not the model's hidden intent.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_security_phase3.ApprovalTests -v

docs.title: 4b. Generated tools and agents
docs.text:
Threat. A model or user proposes a tool/agent that silently gains execution rights, bypasses review, or changes after approval.

Controls

  • Generated artifacts are stored with a checksum and a draft → approved → enabled lifecycle.
  • Only administrators can approve, reject, enable or disable.
  • Drafts and disabled artifacts are never registered and are re-checked at every invocation, even if an old object remains in a registry.
  • Generated tools support only one safe HTTPS GET with an explicit host allow-list, no custom headers/secrets, SSRF checks, bounded output and optional JSON validation.
  • Generated agents run with an allow-listed tool set and bounded steps.
  • Every transition is audited.

docs.title: 5. Plugin and MCP supply chain
docs.text:
Threat. A third-party plugin or MCP server declares one capability, then reads secrets, registers dangerous tools or calls the network.

Controls

  • Plugins declare permissions in their manifest; undeclared permissions fail loading. They run in-process, so they are trusted local code.
  • MCP servers are installed explicitly and can be enabled/disabled.
  • MCP policy supports default, user, role and org allow-lists; the tool executor enforces them per caller.
  • MCP environment/command/URL fields are hidden from the database tools.
  • Installed MCP servers must be explicitly connected; connection failures do not silently grant tools.
  • CI runs secret scanning and a dependency audit.

Residual risk. A malicious plugin that declares the permissions it needs can still act within them. Install only code you trust.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_p4 -v

docs.title: 6. Backup and key loss
docs.text:
Threat. The database is lost, corrupted or ransomware-encrypted; the master key is lost; a backup is untested and cannot be restored.

Controls

  • The worker schedules a consistent database backup every 24 hours and prunes old copies (jobs.backup_keep).
  • scripts/backup.sh / scripts/restore.sh wrap the same helpers.
  • Restore keeps a pre-restore safety copy.
  • scripts/backup_drill.py creates a backup, copies it, opens it and runs PRAGMA integrity_check, recording RPO/RTO without touching the live DB.
  • The master key is stored separately and can be supplied by env or file.

Residual risk. Backups are not application-encrypted as a whole. Protect the backup directory with OS permissions and disk encryption, and back up the master key separately from the database.

Verify

python3 scripts/backup_drill.py --json
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_backup_drill -v

docs.title: 7. Audit tampering and data leakage in exports
docs.text:
Threat. An administrator exports logs containing passwords, bearer tokens or raw tool payloads and shares them; or an attacker deletes/edits audit rows.

Controls

  • Authentication, admin, device and approval actions are appended to auth_audit; tool calls go to tool_calls.
  • /api/v1/admin/audit/export redacts secret-looking keys and token-shaped values before JSON/CSV serialization and records the export itself.
  • Session hashes are redacted; payload columns are not part of the export.
  • Database tools hide secret columns and internal tables.

Residual risk. Audit tables live in the same database. A host-level attacker who can write the database can alter them; ship logs off-host for high-assurance deployments.

Verify

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_security_phase3.AuditExportApiTests -v

docs.title: 8. Container escape and host sensing
docs.text:
Threat. An agent escapes the Bubblewrap sandbox or the container and reaches the host; or users assume Docker gives full host telemetry.

Controls

  • The container runs as a non-root user with no-new-privileges, all Linux capabilities dropped, a read-only root filesystem and a small noexec /tmp.
  • No Docker socket mount, no privileged, only the data volume and config.yaml.
  • Bubblewrap provides a private filesystem namespace with resource limits.
  • Process limits bound fork bombs.

Residual risk. Bubblewrap and containers share the host kernel. They are not a VM boundary. Host sensors inside Docker see only what the container exposes: the container's CPU/memory/process view, mounted paths and network namespace. Phone/desktop signals come from VIRA Link, not from the server container.

Verify

docker compose config | grep -E 'privileged|cap_drop|read_only|no-new-privileges|docker.sock'
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_sandbox -v

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: HTTP API reference
docs.text: VIRA Server exposes a FastAPI application. The reference below is generated from the live OpenAPI schema, so it always matches the code.

docs.title: Interactive API docs
docs.text:
When a server is running, the same schema is available at:

  • /docs — Swagger UI
  • /redoc — ReDoc
  • /openapi.json — raw schema

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Generated at build time

openapi.json on this page is produced by python scripts/export_openapi.py during the documentation build. It is not edited by hand. If the schema is missing here, the build step failed — check the docs workflow logs.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
VIRA reads config.yaml from the repository root (override with VIRA_CONFIG). The dashboard can edit it and reload the runtime.

The canonical file is config.yaml. The table below is a map of the top-level sections, not a replacement for the file's inline comments.

Section Controls kernel Name, checkpoint, log, plugin, module and sensor directories plugins Plugin search paths, write-tool permission and plugin data directory auth Session secret, cookie name, session lifetime, HTTPS-only and database URL devices Device credential lifetime, local device backend and event policy event_bus Event queue size scheduler Tick interval sandbox Backend, workspace root, network, timeouts, CPU/memory limits tools Tool workspace root security Default tool permissions rate_limits Enablement and per-route limits jobs Worker interval, rollup and retention windows, backup count agent_scheduler Proactive schedule tick, concurrency, locks, timeout and quiet-hours defaults notifications In-app notification delivery and optional webhook provider metrics Enablement and retention sensors Per-sensor enablement and polling settings llm Default model and provider/model catalogue agents Enabled agents and their settings mcp_server MCP server command and permissions database_mcp Built-in read-only database MCP server agent_policy Persisted-agent loading and allowed modules

docs.title: Environment overrides
docs.text:
Docker deployments use .env for the values that most often change:

Variable Purpose Default VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS Interface the server binds to 127.0.0.1 VIRA_PORT Host port 8000 VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL Model the bundled Ollama pulls qwen3.5:9b VIRA_CONFIG Path to an alternate config.yaml config.yaml VIRA_TRUSTED_PROXIES Proxy IPs trusted for forwarded headers 127.0.0.1

See .env.example for the full set.

docs.title: Proactive agents and notifications
docs.text:
agent_scheduler:
  enabled: true
  tick_seconds: 20          # how often due schedules are claimed
  max_concurrent: 2         # simultaneous scheduled agent runs
  max_runs_per_tick: 10
  lock_seconds: 300         # crash-safe claim expiry
  run_timeout_seconds: 240
  notify_on_error: true

notifications:
  webhook_url: ""           # optional external delivery
  webhook_timeout_seconds: 10
  max_attempts: 3
  push_provider: "relay"    # relay | fcm
  push_relay_url: ""        # gateway mode
  push_relay_token: ""
  push_timeout_seconds: 10
  fcm_service_account_file: ""   # FCM mode
  fcm_project_id: ""

Schedules are created per user through /api/v1/agent-schedules. Each schedule can carry a structured input object (for example {"mode": "evening"}) that is merged into the agent's TaskRequest.input. See Proactive agents for the workflow.

docs.title: Security-critical keys
docs.text:
Before exposing VIRA beyond localhost

  • Set auth.secret_key to a long random value.
  • Set auth.https_only: true and terminate TLS at a reverse proxy.
  • Review tools and security.default_permissions.
  • Keep port 8000 behind the reverse proxy.

The Bubblewrap sandbox is for development workloads, not hostile code. Use a container or VM for a stronger boundary. See Sandbox execution environments for the full lifecycle, operations and policy reference.

docs.title: Sandbox keys
docs.text:
Key Default Purpose backend bubblewrap Execution backend (Bubblewrap is the supported backend) root /AgentWorkspace Writable root for sandbox workspaces and archives bwrap_binary bwrap Override the Bubblewrap executable path network_enabled false Default outbound network access timeout_seconds 900 Maximum wall clock per command max_processes 128 Process/thread headroom cpu_seconds 600 RLIMIT_CPU memory_mb 2048 RLIMIT_AS allow_package_install true Enable pip/npm installs allow_shell true Allow shell command strings (bash -lc) workspace_quota_mb 2048 Soft quota for project files max_output_bytes 200000 Per-stream output cap

Individual sandboxes may override these values at creation with the policy argument of the sandbox tool. security.approvals still gates destructive operations.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Docker and deployment
  • Framework config reference
  • LLM providers

docs.title: Event reference
docs.text:
All VIRA events share one structure, defined in vira/kernel/event_bus.py. Events use a domain.entity.action naming convention and are published through the EventDispatcher so security and the pipeline run first.

For the full dataclass, priority levels and publishing examples, see Event standard.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text: Namespace Examples Emitted by sensor.* sensor.hardware.state, sensor.system.state Sensors kernel.* kernel.ready, kernel.shutdown Kernel agent.* agent.registered, agent.unregistered AgentManager user.* user.message, user.activity User-activity sensor / API fs.* fs.file.created, fs.file.modified, fs.file.deleted FileSystemSensor workflow.* workflow.started, workflow.completed, workflow.failed WorkflowEngine memory.* memory.stored, memory.retrieved MemoryManager tool.* tool.invoked, tool.result ToolExecutor device.* device.enrolled, device.focus.session Device service / VIRA Link

docs.title: Priority levels
docs.text: Priority Value When to use LOW 0 Background metrics, periodic logs NORMAL 1 Default for sensor readings HIGH 2 User-triggered actions CRITICAL 3 Security violations, kernel errors, OOM signals

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
Set durable=True on state-changing events. The dispatcher records them in the SQLite outbox before delivery and the kernel retries pending rows after restart. High-frequency sensor telemetry stays non-durable by default.

Consumers that update durable state should use vira.kernel.handle_idempotently so a retried event is applied once per consumer.

docs.title: VIRA User Manual
docs.text: This manual is for people who want to run and use VIRA. No source changes are required.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Getting started — install the server and open the dashboard
  • Five-minute proof — chat, live tool calls and the database boundary
  • One-command install — Linux, macOS and Windows installers
  • Docker and deployment — Compose, Ollama, GPU and operations
  • VIRA Link client — the device companion app
  • Platform capability matrix — artifacts, collectors, signing and uninstall per platform
  • Choose a local model — tiers by RAM/GPU, cloud fallback and the tool-use warning
  • Security overview — controls, evidence and limits
  • Troubleshooting — common install and runtime problems

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A computer, NAS or server that can run Docker (8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB+ recommended)
  • Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Compose v2+
  • About 6–10 GB free disk for images and models
  • Optionally, a phone or desktop for VIRA Link

You do not need VIRA Link to use the dashboard or chat.

docs.title: VIRA Link client
docs.text:
VIRA Link is the Flutter device companion for a VIRA server. It enrolls a device, captures only the signals you enable, stores every event in a local outbox and syncs to the server when it is reachable.

It runs as an Android APK, iOS app, web PWA, Linux AppImage, Windows desktop executable and macOS (Apple Silicon) app. See the platform capability matrix for what each platform can collect and which artifact is published.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Signs in with a normal VIRA user account.
  • Enrolls the device and stores its one-time credential in the platform keystore or keychain.
  • Captures only the signals you enable: usage, focus, battery, screen/session, device health and desktop idle.
  • Writes events to a durable local outbox before any network call, so it works offline and drains automatically when the server returns.
  • Shows local Insights — screen time, unlocks, top apps, focus breakdown and rest suggestions.
  • Agent Inbox — proactive agent results, unread notifications, agent recipe cards, schedule creation/editing, pause/resume, delete, next-run times, run-now and run history.
  • Native agent notifications — a live notification stream while VIRA Link is running, with an OS permission toggle in Settings. Notification taps open the Agent Inbox. Builds with Firebase options also register an FCM token for delivery while the app is closed.
  • Polls server-to-device commands such as pause/resume capture, config update and queue flush.
  • Lists, renames and revokes devices linked to your account.

docs.title: Get the app
docs.text: The client is built from the client/ directory in this repository. Build outputs are produced by the client workflow.

docs.title: Build and run from source
docs.text:
cd client
flutter pub get
flutter run -d chrome       # web
flutter run -d linux        # Linux desktop
flutter run -d macos        # macOS desktop (Apple Silicon)
flutter run                 # connected Android/iOS device

Set the server URL to an address reachable from the device, for example http://192.168.1.20:8000. Keep auth.https_only: false only for local HTTP development; use HTTPS when the server is reachable from other machines.

docs.title: Server URL and networking
docs.text:
• On the same machine, http://localhost:8000 works for the desktop and web build.
  • On a phone, use the server's LAN address, not localhost.
  • If the server binds only to 127.0.0.1, other devices cannot connect. Set VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 in .env and restart.

For developer-level details — module layout, collectors and API contract — see the client README.

docs.title: Five-minute proof
docs.text:
This is the fastest way to see what VIRA actually does: authenticated chat, a real agent tool loop, live tool activity and a read-only database boundary.

Your browser does not support embedded video. Download the MP4.

Demo recording: 12 seconds. The transcript below is the longer written version.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• VIRA Server is running (http://localhost:8000 by default).
  • The first admin account has been created in the browser.
  • A model is available and the Chatbot agent is enabled.
  • Python 3.11+ is available (the demo script uses only the standard library).

If you installed with the one-command installer, the repository is usually at ~/vira.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd ~/vira

export VIRA_USERNAME="your-admin-username"
export VIRA_PASSWORD="your-admin-password"

python3 scripts/demo.py

On a remote server:

python3 scripts/demo.py --url http://192.168.1.20:8000

Ask one custom question instead:

python3 scripts/demo.py --ask "Which agents are enabled?"

docs.title: What it proves
docs.text:
1. Authentication works. The script signs in with a normal VIRA session.
  2. The agent loop works. The Chatbot chooses tools instead of guessing.
  3. Database tools work. Device questions are answered from the live database, not from model memory.
  4. The boundary is real. The final step shows write queries and secret-column reads being rejected before they reach the database.

Example output:

VIRA five-minute proof
Server: http://localhost:8000
[1/4] Signing in
  ✓ signed in as vishal
[2/4] Creating a demo conversation
  ✓ conversation ready
[3/4] Asking the Chatbot

You: How many devices are connected with my account? Use the database tools.
  … Thinking
  → database_account_summary
    ✓ database_account_summary (10 ms)

VIRA: You have 4 devices connected to your account (vishal), and all 4 are
currently active.

You: How many devices are connected with the server? Use the database tools.
  → database_examples
    ✓ database_examples (6 ms)
  → database_query
    ✓ database_query (8 ms)

VIRA: There are 4 devices connected with the server, and all 4 are currently
active.

[4/4] Checking the read-only database boundary
  ✓ rejected: DELETE FROM devices — Only SELECT or WITH queries are allowed.
  ✓ rejected: UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' — Only SELECT or WITH queries are allowed.
  ✓ rejected: SELECT password_hash FROM users — Restricted identifier(s): password_hash
  ✓ allowed: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM devices

Answers depend on your own device count and data.

docs.title: If it fails
docs.text:
Symptom Next step Cannot reach ... Check curl http://localhost:8000/livez; start the server. HTTP 401 Check the username/password, or create the admin in the browser first. HTTP 503 The Chatbot agent is disabled or no model is available. The model is slow Local model speed depends on hardware; the default e4b model is fast, larger models can take 20–60 seconds per answer. Tool calls repeat or output is malformed Run python -m vira doctor, then try a larger local model or a cloud provider. See Choose a local model. The chat UI shows a failure Use Retry, Switch model & retry (administrator) or Show what failed in the recovery panel.

Run the doctor first when a first session fails:

python -m vira doctor

It checks the model, its context size, Ollama, the port, the Chatbot, the database and the master key, and prints a fix for each problem.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text:
The read-only database tools are documented in Database tools. Custom SQL is administrator-only, opens a read-only connection, accepts one SELECT/WITH statement, and blocks writes, secret columns and internal tables.

Run the dedicated tests any time:

python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_database_query -v

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
VIRA has two pieces:

  • VIRA Server — the API, dashboard, chat, agents, tools, memory and scheduler. It runs as a Linux container through Docker, on Linux, macOS or Windows.
  • VIRA Link — the optional device companion that collects usage, focus, battery and health signals. It connects to VIRA Server.

docs.title: One-command install (recommended)
docs.text:
Linux and macOS:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Windows PowerShell:

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

The installer detects your OS, architecture, memory, free disk and GPU, installs or checks Docker, chooses a suitable Ollama model, downloads VIRA, starts the server and worker, pulls the model and prints the dashboard URL.

Open the printed URL — by default http://localhost:8000 — and create your account on first run.

Before the first chat, check the whole path:

python -m vira doctor

It verifies Docker, Ollama, the selected model and context, the port, the Chatbot, the database and the master key. If the model is too small for your hardware, see Choose a local model.

Review before you run

The installers are plain shell and PowerShell scripts in scripts/. Read them first if you prefer to know exactly what runs on your machine.

docs.title: Manual install with Docker
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA.git
cd VIRA
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build

Then pull the default model:

docker compose exec ollama ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

Open http://localhost:8000.

For GPU, native-Ollama and development variants, see Docker and deployment.

docs.title: Connect a device
docs.text:
1. Install VIRA Link on the phone or desktop. See VIRA Link.
  2. Sign in with the same VIRA account.
  3. Approve the signals you want to share. VIRA Link captures nothing that you have not enabled.

The dashboard and chat work without VIRA Link.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• One-command install options
  • Docker, Ollama and GPU
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Choose a local model
docs.text:
VIRA ships with qwen3.5:9b through Ollama. That is the recommended first-run model: it follows the tool protocol reliably and fits an 8–16 GB machine.

The Chatbot drives tools by emitting small JSON calls. Very small models can chat well and still fail that job by repeating calls, inventing tool names or returning malformed JSON. Use this page to pick a model that matches your hardware before you conclude that VIRA is broken.

Tool use below the recommended tier

Tool use may be unreliable below about 4 GB RAM or a 4B-parameter model. If the agent repeats calls, ignores tools or returns broken JSON, move up a tier or use a cloud fallback.

docs.title: Tiers by memory and GPU
docs.text:
Tier RAM Suggested model Tool reliability Notes Minimal 4–8 GB llama3.2:3b Experimental Chat works; multi-step tool use is unreliable. Use for quick tests. Recommended 8–16 GB qwen3.5:9b Good VIRA's default. Strong tool support for its size. Comfortable 16–32 GB qwen2.5:14b Better Better instruction following and tool selection. Large 32 GB+ qwen2.5:32b Best local Best local quality; needs a GPU or a large-memory host to be usable.

The one-command installer chooses a tier from detected RAM. Override it with:

VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL=qwen2.5:14b scripts/install.sh

A GPU does not change the tier names, but it changes what is comfortable: a 24 GB GPU can run the 32B tier quantized while a CPU-only host with the same RAM will be too slow for a good first impression.

docs.title: Context size matters more than parameter count
docs.text:
A model also needs room for the tool catalogue, history and observations. VIRA sets Ollama's num_ctx explicitly (the default config uses 65536) because Ollama's own default can drop the start of a long prompt.

If you use a smaller model, keep num_ctx at 8192 or more:

llm:
  default_model: "qwen3.5:9b"
  models:
    - name: "local-llama"
      provider: "ollama"
      model: "qwen3.5:9b"
      base_url: "http://localhost:11434"
      num_ctx: 8192

Run the doctor to confirm the model is installed and the context is configured:

python -m vira doctor

docs.title: Check your machine first
docs.text:
python -m vira doctor

The doctor checks Docker and Compose, Ollama reachability, the selected model and its context size, port conflicts, the Chatbot agent, database writability and the master key. It prints a fix for every warning or failure. See Troubleshooting for the full list.

docs.title: Cloud fallback
docs.text:
A local model is optional. If your hardware cannot run the recommended tier, or you want faster answers, configure a cloud provider.

OpenAI:

llm:
  default_model: "gpt-4o-mini"
  models:
    - name: "gpt-4o-mini"
      provider: "openai"
      model: "gpt-4o-mini"
      api_key: "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"

export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."

Anthropic:

llm:
  default_model: "claude-3-5-sonnet-latest"
  models:
    - name: "claude-3-5-sonnet-latest"
      provider: "anthropic"
      model: "claude-3-5-sonnet-latest"
      api_key: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."

Reload the runtime from the dashboard after changing config.yaml, or restart VIRA. Provider keys are read from the environment and are never returned from the API.

A larger Ollama host also works:

VIRA_OLLAMA_URL=http://gpu-box.lan:11434 python run.py

docs.title: Switch models without restarting
docs.text:
Administrators can switch the active Ollama model from the chat recovery panel after a failure. The same action is available over the API:

curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/models/select \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "qwen2.5:14b"}'

VIRA saves the choice to config.yaml and updates the running provider. Pull the model first with ollama pull <model>.

docs.title: Measure before you change
docs.text:
Run the tool-use benchmark against your own server and model:

VIRA_USERNAME=you VIRA_PASSWORD=... python3 scripts/benchmark.py --runs 10

The deterministic layer runs in CI. The live layer records whether device, database, RAG and web questions actually selected tools. See the tool-use benchmark for the current baseline.

docs.title: Platform capability matrix
docs.text:
VIRA has two pieces with different platform stories:

  • VIRA Server runs anywhere Docker runs: Linux, macOS and Windows.
  • VIRA Link is the native device companion. Its collectors depend on what the operating system exposes; it reports permission_denied, degraded or unavailable instead of inventing data.

The client roadmap tracks deeper collector work.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
Platform Supported How Linux Yes Docker Compose, one-command installer macOS Yes Docker Desktop or Colima + native Ollama for Metal Windows Yes Docker Desktop + PowerShell installer NAS / homelab Yes Docker Compose on the NAS

Host sensing inside the server container is limited by Docker. App usage, focus, battery and health signals come from VIRA Link on the endpoint, not from the server container. See what host sensing looks like inside Docker.

docs.title: VIRA Link artifacts
docs.text:
Platform Artifact Signing Notes Android *-android.apk Debug-signed unless signing secrets are configured Usage Access is required for app usage iOS *-ios-unsigned.zip Unsigned Sign in Xcode with your Apple credentials Web / PWA *-web.zip HTTPS Best on macOS and any modern browser Linux x86_64 *-linux-x86_64.AppImage — chmod +x, then run Windows x64 *-windows-x64.zip — Unzip and run vira_link.exe macOS *-macos-arm64.zip Unsigned Apple Silicon; right-click → Open the first time

Release artifacts are produced by build-client.yml and published with checksums.txt. Verify downloads:

sha256sum -c checksums.txt        # Linux
shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt    # macOS

docs.title: Collector support
docs.text: Capability Android iOS Linux Windows macOS Web Device/app status Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Network state Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Limited Hardware / health Limited No Yes Partial Partial No App usage Yes (Usage Access) No Yes (active window) Yes (foreground window) Yes (frontmost app) No Screen / session Yes No Partial Partial No Limited Battery Yes No Yes Partial No API-dependent Focus / idle Yes No Yes Yes Yes No Active window — — X11, Sway, Hyprland, KDE; GNOME via extension Yes Yes No Notifications In-app only In-app only In-app only In-app only In-app only In-app only Crash diagnostics Opt-in Opt-in Opt-in Opt-in Opt-in Opt-in

docs.title: macOS support decision
docs.text:
VIRA Link now has a native macOS target built by the release workflow on macos-latest (Apple Silicon). It supports signing in, enrollment, sync, chat, insights, desktop active-window capture and the same permission diagnostics as the other desktop builds.

Known limits:

  • The published macOS build is unsigned and arm64. Right-click → Open the first time, or sign/notarize it with your Apple Developer credentials.
  • Intel Macs should use the web/PWA client. An Intel desktop artifact is not part of the release matrix yet.
  • macOS app-sandbox entitlements are limited to network client/server and the app's keychain group. VIRA Link does not request screen recording or accessibility permissions; those signals are unavailable and report honestly.
  • The server itself still runs on macOS through Docker; native Ollama on the host is recommended for Metal acceleration.

docs.title: Permissions and notifications
docs.text:
• The first-run permission banner on Overview lists signals that need an OS permission and opens the right settings page where the platform supports it.
  • Settings → Permissions and notifications repeats the list, explains every unavailable signal and lets you turn in-app break reminders on or off.
  • OS notifications are not scheduled by this build. VIRA uses in-app reminders. It will request notification permission only when scheduled notifications are implemented, so it does not ask for a permission it cannot use.
  • Every collector remains independently disableable. Turning one off stops new events; queued events still sync.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Crash and error diagnostics are off by default. When enabled:

  • reports stay on the device unless you press Send diagnostic report;
  • only app version, platform/device type/OS version, sync state, collector statuses and redacted error text are included;
  • credentials, server URL, device ID, username, chat content and event payloads are excluded;
  • the client redacts token-shaped strings and URLs before storing or sending;
  • the server applies a second redaction pass and stores the report in the administrator audit view (/api/v1/admin/diagnostics).

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Platform Clean removal Android Uninstall the app from the launcher or system settings iOS Remove the app; delete the Keychain item if you used a shared keychain Web Clear site data for the VIRA server origin Linux Delete the AppImage; remove ~/.local/share/com.vira.link if present Windows Delete the unzipped folder and %APPDATA%\com.vira.link macOS Move vira_link.app to the Trash; delete the app container if prompted

Revoke the device first in VIRA Link → Settings → Device lifecycle → Sign out and unlink, or from the server dashboard, so the credential cannot be reused.

docs.title: Proactive agents and schedules
docs.text:
VIRA can run an agent on a schedule, not only when you send a chat message. Schedules are opt-in, user-scoped and durable across restarts.

This first release ships the scheduling, delivery and safety prerequisites for the five daily-use agents in the agent roadmap. You can already schedule any installed agent; the five recommended agents are delivered next.

docs.title: Where you see results
docs.text:
• Web dashboard → Inbox: unread agent results, schedule list, schedule create/edit/pause/delete, run-now and run history.
  • VIRA Link → Inbox (mobile and desktop client): unread agent updates, full result text, agent recipe cards, schedule creation/editing, pause/resume, delete, next run time, run-now and run history.
  • Native notifications in VIRA Link while it is running, after the user enables the permission in Settings.
  • API: GET /api/v1/notifications, GET /api/v1/agent-schedules, GET /api/v1/agent-schedules/{id}/runs.
  • Webhook or push relay (optional): forward notifications to a desktop notifier, FCM/APNs gateway or automation service.

docs.title: Recommended agents
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/agent-recipes returns the onboarding catalog:

Agent Daily trigger Architecture Status Morning Brief morning single available Focus & Wellbeing Coach morning, mid-day, evening single available Second Brain capture + weekly consolidation single available Chief of Staff morning and evening centralized available Household & Life Admin morning, evening, weekly review single → centralized weekly available

Each recipe includes its pitch, required tools, default schedule and current status.

docs.title: Morning Brief
docs.text:
The Morning Brief agent is installed as morning-brief. It collects the configured context tools (by default user_context and insights for the last day), adds recent memory, and writes a short brief with three sections:

  1. Today — priorities supported by the collected context.
  2. Device & focus — battery, device health and focus summary.
  3. Do first — at most three concrete actions.

Missing tools are shown as UNAVAILABLE rather than guessed. If the model is down, a deterministic fallback still produces the brief.

To use a calendar, task or email MCP connector, add its tool name to the agent config:

agents:
  - name: MorningBriefAgent
    module: vira.agent.Agents.morning_brief
    class: MorningBriefAgent
    agent_id: morning-brief
    enabled: true
    config:
      context_tools:
        - name: user_context
        - name: insights
          params: {days: 1}
        - name: mcp_server.calendar_today
        - name: mcp_server.tasks_due

Then schedule it:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "morning-brief", "name": "Morning brief",
       "message": "Write my morning brief.", "schedule_type": "daily",
       "time_of_day": "07:30", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata"}'

docs.title: Focus & Wellbeing Coach
docs.text:
Installed as focus-coach. One agent supports four modes through the schedule input:

Mode What it produces morning A focus plan for today with 2–4 blocks and a break rule checkin A two-sentence mid-day observation and nudge evening An evening review with one win, one adjustment and tomorrow’s first block weekly A weekly report with totals, category balance and three recommendations

Recommendations cite measured numbers from insights and user_context. Goals come from memory. Weekly mode hides specific app names by default; categories and totals remain.

# Evening review every day
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "focus-coach", "name": "Evening review",
       "message": "Review my focus today.", "schedule_type": "daily",
       "time_of_day": "18:30", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",
       "input": {"mode": "evening"}}'

# Weekly report on Sunday evening, with app names hidden
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "focus-coach", "name": "Weekly focus",
       "message": "Write my weekly report.", "schedule_type": "weekly",
       "weekday": 6, "time_of_day": "19:00",
       "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata", "input": {"mode": "weekly"}}'

Quiet hours are applied by the scheduler, so a check-in or break reminder never fires during the user’s quiet window.

docs.title: Second Brain
docs.text:
Installed as second-brain. It supports three modes:

Mode What it does capture Saves the note as verified personal knowledge ask Answers from stored notes with numbered citations and dates correct Creates a superseding revision of an existing item consolidate Reports duplicates, stale items and low-confidence items without deleting anything

Capture is normally done from chat: “Remember that the vendor contract renews in March.” The important rule is that capture only stores what the user explicitly asked to remember.

# Weekly consolidation report
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "second-brain", "name": "Second brain review",
       "message": "Consolidate my notes.", "schedule_type": "weekly",
       "weekday": 6, "time_of_day": "19:00",
       "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata", "input": {"mode": "consolidate"}}'

Capture writes to the existing scoped knowledge base, so the knowledge API, export and delete flows continue to apply. Corrections create a new revision via PATCH /api/v1/knowledge/items/{item_id}; the previous revision is retained and marked deprecated.

docs.title: Chief of Staff
docs.text:
Installed as chief-of-staff. It collects configured email, calendar and task connectors in parallel, extracts source-linked action items, and drafts replies. It does not send anything; sent is always 0 and drafts are returned for a human to approve.

VIRA includes a local, read-only reference connector at examples/mcp/office_server.py. It reads:

data/office/emails.json
data/office/calendar.json
data/office/tasks.json

Register it as the MCP server office, then configure the tools:

agents:
  - name: ChiefOfStaffAgent
    module: vira.agent.Agents.chief_of_staff
    class: ChiefOfStaffAgent
    agent_id: chief-of-staff
    enabled: true
    config:
      mode: morning
      context_tools:
        - {name: office.email_inbox, role: email}
        - {name: office.calendar_today, role: calendar}
        - {name: office.tasks_due, role: tasks}

Schedule a morning triage:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "chief-of-staff", "name": "Morning triage",
       "message": "Triage my day.", "schedule_type": "daily",
       "time_of_day": "08:00", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",
       "input": {"mode": "morning"}}'

If a connector is unavailable, the brief lists it under Unavailable and continues with the sources that worked.

docs.title: Household & Life Admin
docs.text:
Installed as household. It reads the shared household notes, reminders and open chores, then produces a morning plan, evening check or weekly review. Weekly mode fans out meals, budget and chores to parallel workers.

# Get the household id
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/households \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

# Morning plan for every member, each with their own quiet hours
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "household", "name": "Household morning",
       "message": "Plan the household day.", "schedule_type": "daily",
       "time_of_day": "07:00", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",
       "quiet_hours_start": "22:00", "quiet_hours_end": "06:30",
       "input": {"mode": "morning", "household_id": "<household-id>"}}'

Each member creates their own schedule, so the weekly review respects each person’s quiet hours. Household reads are membership-checked; non-members get a permission error rather than partial data.

docs.title: See what can be scheduled
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules/agents \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

This lists installed agents with their coordination architecture.

docs.title: Create your first schedule
docs.text:
The easiest path is VIRA Link → Inbox → Schedules → Add schedule. Pick an agent recipe, choose the time, timezone, mode and quiet hours, then save.

The same flow is available over the API:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "agent_id": "morning-brief",
    "name": "Morning brief",
    "message": "Summarise my day: priorities, device health and focus context. Keep it short.",
    "schedule_type": "daily",
    "time_of_day": "07:30",
    "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",
    "quiet_hours_start": "22:00",
    "quiet_hours_end": "07:00",
    "channels": ["inapp"],
    "task_profile": {"decomposability": 0.7, "sequential_dependencies": 0.2}
  }'

The response includes next_run_at in UTC. The scheduler evaluates daily and weekly times in the schedule's IANA timezone.

docs.title: Schedule types
docs.text:
Type Fields Example daily time_of_day (HH:MM) Every day at 07:30 weekly weekday (0=Monday) + time_of_day Sunday at 19:00 interval interval_minutes Every 90 minutes

Quiet hours apply to all types. A run scheduled inside the quiet window moves to the end of the window instead of being dropped.

docs.title: Manage schedules
docs.text:
# List
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

# Change the time or pause it
curl -s -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules/<id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"time_of_day": "08:00", "enabled": true}'

# Run now (queued for the next scheduler tick)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules/<id>/run \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

# Inspect runs and results
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules/<id>/runs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

# Delete
curl -s -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/api/v1/agent-schedules/<id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

Deleting a schedule stops future runs. It does not delete runs already recorded or notifications already delivered.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Every scheduled run creates an in-app notification with the agent result. In-app notifications are available immediately:

curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/notifications \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/notifications/<id>/read \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <session>"

docs.title: Native notifications in VIRA Link
docs.text:
VIRA Link keeps a live notification stream open while it is running and shows native alerts for new agent results. Enable the OS permission from Settings → Permissions and notifications → Agent notifications → Enable. Tapping an alert opens the Agent Inbox.

This covers foreground and desktop use. Delivery while the app is fully closed needs a remote push gateway (next section). The live stream is held by the API process serving the client; if you run several API replicas, use the push relay or webhook for cross-process delivery.

docs.title: External delivery
docs.text:
External delivery uses a JSON webhook or a push provider. Two push modes are supported:

  • push_provider: "relay" forwards {tokens, notification} to a gateway.
  • push_provider: "fcm" sends directly through Firebase Cloud Messaging HTTP v1 using a service account. FCM also delivers to iOS/macOS when APNs is configured in the Firebase project.
notifications:
  webhook_url: "https://notify.example.com/vira"
  webhook_timeout_seconds: 10
  max_attempts: 3
  push_provider: "fcm"                 # relay | fcm
  push_relay_url: ""
  push_relay_token: ""
  push_timeout_seconds: 10
  fcm_service_account_file: "secrets/firebase-service-account.json"
  fcm_project_id: "your-firebase-project"

For FCM, build VIRA Link with the Firebase app values:

flutter run \
  --dart-define=VIRA_FIREBASE_API_KEY=... \
  --dart-define=VIRA_FIREBASE_APP_ID=... \
  --dart-define=VIRA_FIREBASE_MESSAGING_SENDER_ID=... \
  --dart-define=VIRA_FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID=...

The client registers its FCM token through POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/push-registration. Android receives notifications when the app is fully closed. iOS/macOS additionally need an APNs key uploaded to the Firebase project and the app built with the Push Notifications capability.

The relay mode is still available for other push gateways and for deployments that do not want a Firebase project:

{"tokens": [{"device_id": "...", "platform": "android", "token": "..."}],
 "notification": {"id": "...", "title": "...", "body": "...", "data": {}}}

docs.title: Safety and limits
docs.text:
• Schedules are scoped to the authenticated user. Another user cannot read, change, run or delete them.
  • Scheduled runs use the same tool permissions, approval gates and audit trail as chat.
  • A run has a timeout (agent_scheduler.run_timeout_seconds) and the scheduler bounds concurrency (max_concurrent) and runs per tick.
  • If the server restarts, due schedules are retried instead of lost; locks expire so a crashed run does not block forever.
  • Missed days are not backfilled: after downtime the schedule runs once and advances to the next future occurrence, so a returning user is not flooded with old briefs.
  • Disable a schedule with "enabled": false instead of deleting it if you only want a pause.

docs.title: Security and privacy overview
docs.text:
VIRA is local-first by design, but “local” is not a complete security model. This page describes what is implemented, what it protects, and where the limits are.

For reporting a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md. The engineering threat model is in the developer manual.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Local-first: the server, database, model and device data run on infrastructure you control. Cloud model providers are optional.
  • Least privilege: users, devices, agents, tools and plugins have separate identities and permissions.
  • Explicit consent: device collectors are opt-in and can be revoked per device.
  • Auditable: authentication, admin actions and tool calls are recorded.
  • Bounded execution: tool calls have permissions, timeouts and (where available) a sandbox.
  • No security theatre: known limitations are listed below.

docs.title: Authentication and sessions
docs.text:
• Passwords and recovery codes are hashed with bcrypt; plaintext passwords are never stored.
  • User sessions are random tokens stored as hashes with an expiry. Logout, password reset and admin disable/delete revoke sessions.
  • Device credentials are separate from user sessions, scoped, expiring and revocable. Raw device tokens are shown once and stored as hashes.
  • The session cookie is signed with auth.secret_key. Set a random value before exposing the server.
  • auth.https_only must be enabled when the server is behind HTTPS/TLS.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
• Users have admin or user roles.
  • Device access is granted per user/device through explicit access rows.
  • Admin-only routes cover users, fleet, audit, jobs, backups, health, metrics, configuration, plugins, MCP servers and updates.
  • Tool execution checks the tool permission, the agent’s runtime permission, and installed-MCP allow/deny policies.
  • Database tools add a further role gate: custom SQL requires an administrator; every user can read only their own account summary.

docs.title: Destructive tool approvals
docs.text:
Destructive calls do not execute immediately. Shell, filesystem writes, sandbox writes/execute/install and any tool configured as destructive create a single-use approval request and return APPROVAL_REQUIRED to the agent.

  • The request records the tool, action, redacted arguments, caller, agent, run and expiry (30 minutes by default).
  • The dashboard Security page shows the pending queue with Approve/Deny buttons; the same actions are available at /api/v1/approvals.
  • The next identical call from the same user consumes the approval once.
  • Every decision is written to the audit log.
  • Approvals are enabled by security.approvals.enabled in config.yaml; the tool/operation lists can be extended without changing code.

This is a human gate, not a sandbox. It limits accidental or injected destructive actions and leaves an audit trail.

docs.title: Device sensing and consent
docs.text:
• VIRA Link collectors are individually enabled and can be disabled at any time.
  • Consent is stored per device and collector with purpose and retention.
  • The ingestion path rejects events for collectors that are not consented (consent_denied) and applies retention overrides.
  • The server itself is registered as a device, but local sensors are separate from remote device data.
  • Inside Docker, host sensor visibility is limited by the container boundary. This is a deliberate safety trade-off, not a promise of full host telemetry.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
• Sensitive configuration values and device event payloads are encrypted with Fernet using a master key.
  • The default key file is data/.vira_master_key. VIRA_MASTER_KEY and VIRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE can override it.
  • Back up the master key separately. Without it, encrypted values cannot be recovered.
  • This is field-level encryption for sensitive values, not full-database encryption. Protect the host and the database file with OS permissions and disk encryption as well.

docs.title: Container and sandbox
docs.text:
• The server image runs as a non-root user.
  • The default Compose services use no-new-privileges: true, drop all Linux capabilities, run with a read-only root filesystem and a small noexec /tmp tmpfs, and set process limits.
  • The default Compose file does not use privileged, does not mount the Docker socket, and mounts only the data volume and config.yaml.
  • The Bubblewrap sandbox gives agents a private filesystem namespace with CPU, memory, process and timeout limits. It is designed for development workloads, not for running hostile code. Use a container or VM for a stronger boundary.
  • Sandbox workspaces are persistent and owned by an agent plus the signed-in user; explicit sandbox IDs owned by another user are rejected. Commands run with a cleared environment, read-only system paths, --cap-drop ALL, and only the workspace and artifacts mounts writable.
  • The shipped config.yaml lists sandbox in security.approvals.safe_tools, so a ChatAgent can build, write and execute inside its isolated environment without a prompt for every file or command. Remove it from safe_tools to restore per-call approval. Read-only inspection operations never need approval, and shell/filesystem tools remain gated regardless.
  • Plugins run in-process and are treated as trusted local code. Install only plugins you trust.

docs.title: What host sensing looks like inside Docker
docs.text:
Docker is a boundary, not magic. Inside the server container:

  • hardware/CPU/memory/process sensors see the container's view of the host, subject to cgroup limits and the container's PID namespace;
  • filesystem sensors see only paths mounted into the container (by default the data volume and /app);
  • network sensors see the container network namespace;
  • phone/desktop signals (app usage, focus, battery, health) come from VIRA Link, not from the server container.

If you need richer host telemetry, run trusted sensors outside the container and ingest through the normal consent-gated event path. Do not mount the Docker socket or run the container privileged to work around this.

docs.title: Database tools
docs.text:
The read-only database MCP server (database_query) is deliberately constrained:

  • one SELECT or WITH statement;
  • read-only SQLite connection (mode=ro, query_only) or read-only PostgreSQL session;
  • write keywords, multiple statements, PRAGMA, ATTACH, secret columns and internal tables rejected;
  • maximum 200 rows, statement timeout and result-size caps;
  • custom SQL restricted to administrators;
  • caller identity injected by the agent loop, never trusted from the model;
  • {{caller_user_id}} for the signed-in user.

See Database tools.

docs.title: Audit and observability
docs.text:
• auth_audit records authentication, admin and device actions with allowed/denied status and correlation IDs.
  • tool_calls records tool name, request, result, status, permission decision, duration and agent. Treat this table as sensitive; it can contain tool inputs and outputs.
  • The dashboard exposes audit, metrics, health, jobs and alerts to administrators.
  • Administrators can export a redacted audit trail:
curl -s "http://localhost:8000/api/v1/admin/audit/export?kind=all&format=json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-session>" > vira-audit.json

Secret-looking keys and token-shaped values are replaced with [REDACTED], session hashes are not exported, and the export itself is audited. CSV is available with format=csv; kind is audit, tool_calls or all.

docs.title: Backups, RPO and RTO
docs.text:
• The worker schedules a database backup every 24 hours; this gives a documented RPO target of 24 hours. jobs.backup_keep controls retention.
  • RTO depends on database size and host speed. Measure it on your own data rather than assuming a number.
  • Run the non-destructive drill to record both on your machine:
python3 scripts/backup_drill.py --write docs/dev/runbooks/backup-restore.md

The drill creates a real backup, copies it, opens it independently and runs PRAGMA integrity_check. It never overwrites the live database. - Restore procedure: stop the API and worker, run scripts/restore.sh <backup>, start the services and verify /livez, sign-in and recent conversations. A pre-restore safety copy is kept. - Back up the master key separately. A database backup without data/.vira_master_key (or VIRA_MASTER_KEY) cannot decrypt sensitive fields.

Current drill evidence: backup and restore drill.

docs.title: Supply chain and CI
docs.text:
• The repository CI runs gitleaks secret scanning and pip-audit against requirements.txt on every push and pull request, plus a weekly scheduled run.
  • Release artifacts include checksums where the release workflow produces them.
  • Plugins/MCP servers are third-party code. Review the manifest and permissions before installing.

docs.title: Generated tools and agents
docs.text: Generated artifacts follow draft → approved → enabled and can only be approved/enabled by an administrator. A draft or disabled artifact is never registered and is re-checked at invocation time, so it cannot execute just because a model asked for it. Generated tools are restricted to one HTTPS GET with an explicit host allow-list, no custom headers or secrets, SSRF checks and bounded, optionally JSON-validated output. Generated agents run with an allow-listed tool set and a step budget. Every transition is audited in Agents → Generated tools and agents.

docs.title: Client diagnostics
docs.text: VIRA Link diagnostics are off by default. When enabled, errors are stored locally with a bounded history and are uploaded only when the user chooses Send diagnostic report. The client removes credentials, URLs, token-shaped text, device identifiers, usernames and chat/event content before storage; the server applies a second redaction pass and stores the report in the administrator audit view. See the platform matrix.

docs.title: Network exposure
docs.text:
• By default, Compose publishes port 8000 on 0.0.0.0. To restrict it to the local machine, set VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 in .env.
  • Put VIRA behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy before exposing it beyond a trusted network.
  • Do not publish Ollama (11434) to the internet.
  • Rate limits are configured in config.yaml under rate_limits.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Prompt injection is an open problem. Tool output and retrieved documents are treated as untrusted, but no system can guarantee safe behaviour for every model.
  • The Bubblewrap sandbox is not a virtual-machine boundary.
  • Plugins are trusted in-process code.
  • CORS is intentionally narrow for local HTTP; a production reverse proxy still needs its own policy.
  • SQLite file access is protected by OS permissions, not by application-level encryption of the whole file.
  • There is no formal verification of generated tools or agents. Do not treat “verified” as a current capability.
  • Backups are only as good as the tested restore process. Run the drill.
  • Multi-user isolation has tests, but it is not a formally audited multi-tenant boundary.
  • Approval gates require a human decision and are not a sandbox or a policy engine. A destructive tool outside the configured list is not automatically gated.

docs.title: How to verify
docs.text:
# approvals, isolation, redaction and audit export
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_security_phase3 -v

# multi-user / multi-device isolation and stream ACL
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_multi_device -v

# read-only database tool boundary
python3 -m unittest vira.tests.test_database_query -v

# backup/restore drill
python3 scripts/backup_drill.py --json

# whole suite (recommended before a release)
python3 -m unittest $(ls vira/tests/test_*.py | sed 's#/#.#g; s#\.py$##')

Security-sensitive deployments should also run their own dependency scanning, secret scanning, backup restore drills and penetration testing. The engineering detail for each threat is in the threat model.

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text: VIRA is designed to run on hardware you already own. This page collects the reproducible demo and a few deployment patterns you can copy. Community submissions will be added as they arrive; nothing here is a benchmark of model quality.

docs.title: The five-minute proof
docs.text:
The canonical demo: sign in, ask about your own devices, watch the Chatbot call a read-only database tool, and verify that writes are rejected.

  • Run the demo
  • Tool-use benchmark
  • Agent platform evaluation

docs.title: Deployment patterns
docs.text: These are patterns, not customer stories. Each one uses only features in the current tree.

docs.title: 1. Family NAS assistant
docs.text:
• Docker Compose on a Linux NAS or mini-PC;
  • bundled Ollama with the e4b default model;
  • VIRA Link on family phones for consent-gated usage/focus signals;
  • household users with separate accounts and per-device grants;
  • nightly database backup and a separately stored master key.

Why it works: local-first data, one admin, a small web dashboard and no cloud requirement.

docs.title: 2. Developer workstation companion
docs.text:
• source install or Docker Desktop;
  • native Ollama for Metal on Apple Silicon;
  • workspace-scoped filesystem/shell tools and the sandbox;
  • MCP servers for local tools;
  • approval gates for filesystem writes and sandbox execution.

Why it works: the agent can inspect a project and call tools while destructive actions still require a human decision.

docs.title: 3. Study and focus coach
docs.text:
• VIRA Link on an Android phone with Usage Access;
  • focus sessions and local insight ledgers;
  • the insight_coach and study_coach specialists;
  • daily/weekly summaries from aggregate data.

Why it works: the client aggregates locally and the server stores only the signals the user enabled.

docs.title: 4. Private knowledge assistant
docs.text:
• RAG documents loaded from local notes;
  • a local model or a configured cloud fallback;
  • rag_search plus the read-only database tools;
  • per-user document scope and redacted audit exports.

Why it works: retrieval and history stay on your server; answers can cite the local documents they actually used.

docs.title: Add your deployment
docs.text:
We only publish deployments the owner has allowed us to describe publicly. Open a Showcase submission issue with:

  • the deployment pattern and hardware;
  • which model tier you use;
  • MCP servers/plugins and devices involved;
  • one concrete outcome or lesson;
  • a public link or screenshot if available.

Do not include private hostnames, IPs, tokens, device data or personal details. Submissions are reviewed before publication.

docs.title: What we will not publish
docs.text:
• claims that VIRA is “verified” for generated tools/agents;
  • screenshots with real credentials or personal data;
  • benchmarks without a reproducible command and model/version;
  • deployments the submitter cannot publicly describe.

docs.title: Run the doctor
docs.text:
Before changing anything, run the first-run health check from the VIRA directory:

python -m vira doctor

Or, if you only want a machine-readable report:

python -m vira doctor --json

It checks Docker and Compose, Ollama reachability, the selected model and its context size, port conflicts, the Chatbot agent, database writability and the master key. Every warning or failure prints a suggested fix.

If the Chatbot is slow or makes poor tool choices, read Choose a local model before concluding the server is broken.

docs.title: Docker is missing on Windows
docs.text: Install Docker Desktop, enable WSL2 if prompted, reboot, start Docker Desktop, then re-run the installer.

docs.title: Docker is missing on Linux
docs.text: The one-command installer installs Docker Engine automatically. If it cannot, install Docker from your distribution's repository, then re-run the installer.

docs.title: No GPU
docs.text: VIRA falls back to CPU, which is slower. To use an NVIDIA GPU, see the GPU section of Docker and deployment.

docs.title: Apple Silicon
docs.text: Use native Ollama on macOS (--host-ollama). Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM and cannot use Metal GPU acceleration.

docs.title: Model pull fails
docs.text:
The selected model may not be available under that name. Set VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL in .env, then pull the same name manually:

docker compose exec ollama ollama pull <model>

docs.title: Port is already in use
docs.text: Re-run the installer with --port 8080, or change VIRA_PORT in .env and restart.

docs.title: A device cannot reach the server
docs.text:
• Use the server's LAN address on the device, not localhost.
  • Set VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 in .env and restart.
  • Allow port 8000 through the host firewall.
  • Keep auth.https_only: false only for local HTTP; use HTTPS otherwise.

docs.title: Where are the logs?
docs.text:
docker compose logs -f vira-server
docker compose logs -f worker

Operational endpoints: /health and /metrics on the server.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue at https://github.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/issues with the output of docker compose ps, docker compose logs vira-server and your OS/architecture.

docs.title: Running VIRA with Docker
docs.text: This is the supported cross-platform way to run VIRA Server. The server runs as a Linux container on Linux, macOS or Windows. The VIRA Link client remains a native app so it can reach the device sensors.

docs.title: First: Server vs client
docs.text:
Piece What it is Where it runs VIRA Server API, web dashboard, chat workspace, agents, tools, memory, database, scheduler, admin Docker container (Linux) Ollama Local model HTTP service Docker container or native host service VIRA Link Device companion: collectors, offline ledgers, sync, command polling Native app on each phone/desktop, or its web build Web console Browser UI served by VIRA Server (/dashboard, /chat) Browser; no separate install

The browser UI is part of the server. VIRA Link is the client that produces device telemetry. You do not need VIRA Link to use the dashboard or chat.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker Engine or Docker Desktop
  • Docker Compose v2+
  • About 6–10 GB free disk for models and images
  • 8 GB RAM minimum; 16 GB+ recommended for larger local models

docs.title: 1. Get the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA.git
cd VIRA
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env if needed:

VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
VIRA_PORT=8000
VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL=qwen3.5:9b
  • VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 exposes the server only on this machine.
  • VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 allows other devices on your LAN to connect.
  • VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL must match an Ollama model you pull. The repository default is qwen3.5:9b. If that model is not available from your Ollama registry, use any capable model, for example llama3.2:3b, in both VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL and ollama pull.

docs.title: 2. Start the server and Ollama
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build
# convenience wrapper: ./docker_run.sh

This starts:

  • vira-server — API + web console on port 8000
  • vira-worker — durable jobs, retention, rollups, backups
  • vira-ollama — Ollama on an internal Docker network (not exposed to the host)

docs.title: 3. Pull the model
docs.text:
docker compose --profile setup run --rm model-pull

Or pull a different model manually after editing VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL:

docker compose exec ollama ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

docs.title: 4. Open VIRA
docs.text:
http://localhost:8000

The first visit creates the administrator account. Then:

  • use /dashboard for the control center
  • use /chat for the chat workspace
  • open the server URL from another device using the host's LAN address, for example http://192.168.1.20:8000

docs.title: 5. Connect VIRA Link
docs.text:
Install/open VIRA Link and enter:

Server URL: http://<server-LAN-IP>:8000

Do not use http://localhost:8000 inside a phone or another computer; that points at the client device itself.

docs.title: Ollama connectivity modes
docs.text:
Ollama is just an HTTP service. VIRA Server reads its endpoint from VIRA_OLLAMA_URL:

Mode URL Best for Bundled Ollama container http://ollama:11434 Simplest, CPU-only, Linux/NVIDIA Native Ollama on the host http://host.docker.internal:11434 macOS Metal, existing installs, fastest host GPU Remote GPU server https://ollama.example.internal Teams, shared GPU machine

The default compose.yaml uses the bundled container.

docs.title: Native Ollama on macOS / Windows
docs.text:
Use the host-ollama Compose file:

docker compose -f compose.host-ollama.yaml up -d --build

It adds host.docker.internal automatically. Make sure the native Ollama service accepts connections from Docker:

OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 ollama serve

On macOS with the Ollama app, set the variable for the app session and restart it:

launchctl setenv OLLAMA_HOST "0.0.0.0:11434"

Only expose 11434 on trusted networks. Do not publish it to the internet.

docs.title: Existing native Ollama on Linux
docs.text:
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 ollama serve
docker compose -f compose.host-ollama.yaml up -d --build

Alternative for a local-only setup: network_mode: host on Linux, but that reduces container isolation. Prefer host.docker.internal or the bundled network.

docs.title: Remote Ollama
docs.text:
VIRA_OLLAMA_URL=https://ollama.example.internal

Put the remote endpoint behind TLS, authentication or a VPN. VIRA Server should not expose an unauthenticated model server to the public internet.

docs.title: NVIDIA GPU with bundled Ollama
docs.text:
Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, then:

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.gpu.yaml up -d --build

For Apple Silicon, prefer native Ollama: Docker Desktop runs Linux containers in a VM and does not provide Metal acceleration to the Ollama container.

docs.title: Data and persistence
docs.text:
Named Docker volumes keep state across rebuilds:

vira_vira-data       -> /app/data (database, master key, artifacts, plugins)
vira_ollama-models   -> /root/.ollama (model weights)

VIRA Server's important files:

/app/data/vira.sqlite3          SQLite database
/app/data/.vira_master_key      encryption key for payloads/secrets
/app/data/objects/              local object storage
/app/data/checkpoints/          kernel state
/app/data/plugins/              plugin state/data

docs.title: Back up
docs.text:
mkdir -p backups
docker run --rm \
  -v vira_vira-data:/data \
  -v "$PWD/backups":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'tar czf /backup/vira-data-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tgz -C /data .'

Also run the in-app backup job/settings if you use PostgreSQL or S3.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
docker compose down
docker run --rm \
  -v vira_vira-data:/data \
  -v "$PWD/backups":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'cd /data && tar xzf /backup/vira-data-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tgz'
docker compose up -d

The master key must be in the same backup. Without it, encrypted payloads cannot be recovered.

docs.title: Reset everything (destructive)
docs.text:
docker compose down -v

This deletes the VIRA database, master key, objects and Ollama models.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
git pull
docker compose up -d --build

Database migrations run automatically on server startup. Back up first. Check:

docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail=100 vira

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The server reads config.yaml from the repository, mounted at /app/config.yaml. You can edit it on the host, or through the dashboard configuration page, then restart:

docker compose restart vira worker

If dashboard saves fail on Linux, the container user cannot write the host file. Set VIRA_UID and VIRA_GID in .env to your host UID/GID and rebuild:

VIRA_UID=$(id -u) VIRA_GID=$(id -g) docker compose up -d --build

Environment overrides:

Variable Meaning VIRA_OLLAMA_URL Ollama endpoint used by chat and embeddings VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL Model name override VIRA_BIND_ADDRESS Host bind address for port 8000 VIRA_PORT Host port VIRA_DATABASE_URL PostgreSQL URL instead of SQLite VIRA_MASTER_KEY / VIRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE encryption key override

Before exposing the server beyond localhost:

  • change auth.secret_key
  • enable auth.https_only behind TLS
  • use a reverse proxy (Caddy, Traefik, nginx)
  • keep Ollama private
  • review device consent, tool permissions and quotas
  • back up the master key separately

docs.title: Container hardening and host sensing
docs.text:
The default Compose services already apply:

  • non-root user (VIRA_UID / VIRA_GID);
  • no-new-privileges: true;
  • all Linux capabilities dropped;
  • a read-only root filesystem;
  • a small noexec /tmp tmpfs;
  • process limits;
  • no Docker socket mount and no privileged mode.

Runtime state lives on the vira-data volume. If you add a feature that writes outside that volume, mount an explicit path instead of disabling the read-only root filesystem.

Docker limits host sensing. The server container sees its own CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network view, not the full host. App usage, focus, battery and health signals come from VIRA Link on phones and desktops. See the security overview for the exact boundaries.

Verify the flags Compose will apply:

docker compose config | grep -E 'privileged|cap_drop|read_only|no-new-privileges|docker.sock'

docs.title: Run the working tree in the container
docs.text:
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.dev.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.dev.yaml logs -f vira

docs.title: Run tests in the container
docs.text: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.dev.yaml run --rm vira python -m pytest -q

docs.title: Build only
docs.text:
docker build -t vira:latest .
# or
./docker_build.sh

docs.title: Open a shell
docs.text: docker compose run --rm vira bash

docs.title: Rebuild after code changes
docs.text: docker compose up -d --build vira worker

docs.title: Plugin development
docs.text: Mount a plugin directory into the container and add it to plugins.directories in config.yaml. The container already includes examples/plugins.

docs.title: The server restarts immediately
docs.text:
docker compose logs --tail=120 vira

Common causes: config parse error, unreadable master key, database permission, or a missing Python dependency after a code update (rebuild the image).

docs.title: curl http://localhost:8000/livez works but /health returns 401
docs.text: /livez is the unauthenticated liveness probe. /health is an administrator health endpoint and requires a session. This is intentional.

docs.title: Ollama connection refused
docs.text:
Check the endpoint from inside the VIRA container:

docker compose exec vira python -c "import urllib.request,os; print(urllib.request.urlopen(os.environ['VIRA_OLLAMA_URL']+'/api/tags').status)"

Check the bundled service:

docker compose exec ollama ollama list

If using native Ollama, make sure it is listening on 0.0.0.0:11434 and the host-ollama compose file is in use.

docs.title: Model not found
docs.text:
docker compose exec ollama ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

Then set VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL to the same name and restart vira worker.

docs.title: Port 8000 is already in use
docs.text:
VIRA_PORT=8080

Then docker compose up -d.

docs.title: VIRA Link cannot connect
docs.text: Use the server machine's LAN IP, not localhost, and ensure the host firewall allows port 8000. If using Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows, the server container is reachable through the published host port.

docs.title: Apple Silicon feels slow
docs.text: Docker runs a Linux VM. Use native Ollama on the host with compose.host-ollama.yaml so Ollama can use Metal.

docs.title: Operator cheat sheet
docs.text:
# start
docker compose up -d --build

# pull model
docker compose --profile setup run --rm model-pull

# status / logs
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f vira worker ollama

# restart after config edit
docker compose restart vira worker

# stop
docker compose down

# stop and delete all data/models
docker compose down -v

# native Ollama on macOS/Linux
docker compose -f compose.host-ollama.yaml up -d --build

# NVIDIA GPU
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.gpu.yaml up -d --build

# development
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.dev.yaml up -d --build

docs.title: Related docs
docs.text:
• Architecture
  • Deployment roadmap
  • Plugin SDK
  • P4 ecosystem
  • Client README

docs.title: One-command VIRA Server install
docs.text: These installers are the fastest path for a new user. They detect the operating system, architecture, memory, free disk and GPU, install/check Docker, choose a sensible Ollama model, download VIRA, start the server and worker, and pull the model.

docs.title: Linux and macOS
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

What it does:

  1. Detects Linux distribution or macOS, CPU architecture, RAM and free disk.
  2. Detects NVIDIA/AMD/Apple GPU where possible.
  3. Installs Docker Engine automatically on Linux if needed.
  4. Uses Docker Desktop on macOS if present; otherwise explains the requirement.
  5. Chooses a model based on available RAM.
  6. Downloads VIRA to ~/vira (or updates an existing checkout).
  7. Starts VIRA Server, the worker and Ollama.
  8. Pulls the model and prints the dashboard URL.

Default Ollama mode:

  • Linux: bundled Ollama container
  • macOS: native Ollama on the host, so it can use Metal

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

What it does:

  1. Detects Windows, CPU architecture, RAM, free disk and NVIDIA GPU.
  2. Checks Docker Desktop; tries to install it with winget if missing.
  3. Chooses a model based on available RAM.
  4. Downloads VIRA to %USERPROFILE%\VIRA.
  5. Starts VIRA Server, the worker and bundled Ollama.
  6. Pulls the model and prints the dashboard URL.

Docker Desktop may require WSL2 and a reboot on first install. If the installer stops, start Docker Desktop, reboot if needed, and run the command again.

docs.title: Review before running
docs.text:
The one-liner downloads and executes a script. If you prefer to inspect it:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.sh -o vira-install.sh
less vira-install.sh
bash vira-install.sh --dry-run
bash vira-install.sh

Windows:

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.ps1 -OutFile vira-install.ps1
notepad vira-install.ps1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\vira-install.ps1 -DryRun
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\vira-install.ps1

docs.title: Linux/macOS
docs.text:
# custom location and port
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --dir ~/apps/vira --port 8080

# choose a model
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --model llama3.1:8b

# use native Ollama instead of the container
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --host-ollama

# use a remote Ollama server
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- \
  --ollama-url https://ollama.example.internal

# NVIDIA GPU with bundled Ollama
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --gpu

# plan only
curl -fsSL .../scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --dry-run

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
When using irm | iex, configure with environment variables before running:

$env:VIRA_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\apps\VIRA"
$env:VIRA_PORT = "8080"
$env:VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.1:8b"
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Vishalsng112/VIRA/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

Or download and run with parameters:

.\vira-install.ps1 -Dir "$env:USERPROFILE\apps\VIRA" -Port 8080 -Model llama3.1:8b
.\vira-install.ps1 -DryRun
.\vira-install.ps1 -OllamaMode host -Gpu

Useful parameters: -Dir, -Port, -BindAddress, -Model, -OllamaMode, -OllamaUrl, -Gpu, -NoModel, -NoDockerInstall, -DryRun.

docs.title: After install
docs.text:
Open:

http://localhost:8000

Create the administrator account on first visit. Then use:

  • /dashboard — control center
  • /chat — chat workspace
  • http://<server-LAN-IP>:8000 — server URL for VIRA Link on other devices

VIRA Server is the Dockerized runtime. VIRA Link is the native device companion that collects usage, focus, battery and health data. You do not need VIRA Link to use the dashboard or chat.

docs.title: Change the model later
docs.text:
cd ~/vira
# edit VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL in .env, then
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec ollama ollama pull llama3.1:8b

docs.title: Stop / restart / logs
docs.text:
cd ~/vira
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f vira worker
docker compose restart vira worker
docker compose down

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Stop the containers:

cd ~/vira
docker compose down

Remove everything, including the database, master key and models:

docker compose down -v
rm -rf ~/vira

Windows:

cd $env:USERPROFILE\VIRA
docker compose down -v
Remove-Item $env:USERPROFILE\VIRA -Recurse -Force

docs.title: If the installer cannot continue
docs.text:
• Docker missing on macOS: install Docker Desktop, OrbStack or Colima, start it, then re-run the installer.
  • Docker missing on Windows: install Docker Desktop, enable WSL2 if prompted, reboot, start Docker Desktop, then re-run.
  • No GPU: the installer uses CPU; models will be slower.
  • Apple Silicon: use native Ollama (--host-ollama on macOS). Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM and cannot use Metal GPU acceleration.
  • Model pull fails: the selected model may not be available under that name. Edit VIRA_OLLAMA_MODEL in .env, then pull the same name manually.
  • Port in use: re-run with --port 8080 or change VIRA_PORT in .env.

For deeper deployment, backup, security and developer instructions see Docker and deployment and the architecture diagram.
